title: 自託管 AI 模型更省錢？Cline 實測 Kimi K3 成本優勢，網反駁：按任務算比 Fable 5 貴
summary:
隨著人工智慧模型的算力成本日益高昂，企業是否該選擇「自託管」成為焦點。AI 開發團隊 Cline 昨（20）日 […]

〈自託管 AI 模型更省錢？Cline 實測 Kimi K3 成本優勢，網反駁：按任務算比 Fable 5 貴〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
隨著人工智慧模型的算力成本日益高昂，企業是否該選擇「自託管」成為焦點。AI 開發團隊 Cline 昨（20）日公布最新實測，指出自託管開放權重模型 Kimi K3 最高可節省 25% 成本，並預測這將成為未來企業兼顧價格與資料主權的標準做法。然而，社群對此提出不同見解，認為若以「每任務成本」計算，Kimi 其實比競爭對手 Fable 5 更為昂貴。
（前情提要：Hugging Face 被 AI agent 打穿！最後鑑識模型靠中國開源 GLM 5.2）
（背景補充：歐盟 8 月開鍘：AI 沒「自報身分」最高罰 3% 全球營收，台灣也在範圍內）
在大語言模型（LLM）的軍備競賽中，除了模型本身的效能，API 的調用成本也成為企業導入 AI 時的重大考量。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 20 日，AI 開發團隊 Cline 在社群平台 X 上發布了一項引人注目的實測數據，探討了「自託管（Self-hosting）」開放權重模型相較於直接使用商業 API，究竟能為企業省下多少資金。
Kimi costs ~3-12x cheaper than Fable, but how much more could you save hosting it yourself?
We ran the numbers on Cline’s production traffic, and the results:
~10% savings, 25%+ with time-of-day autoscaling (but this only works if over $500K/year of spend)
We predict… pic.twitter.com/hi4dKDv4L5
— Cline (@cline) July 20, 2026
自託管 Kimi K3 實測：最高可省 25% 成本
Cline 團隊在貼文中指出，以輸入與輸出代幣（Token）的價格來看，Kimi 的成本原本就比競爭對手 Fable 便宜約 3 到 12 倍。但他們更好奇的是：如果企業選擇自己託管模型，還能再進一步壓縮多少成本？
為此，Cline 將其即時生產環境的實際流量，模擬至配備 8 張 B200 GPU 的伺服器節點上進行實測，並仔細測量了首次代幣生成時間（TTFT）、每串流速度以及快取命中率等關鍵指標。結果顯示，採取自託管模式大約能帶來 10% 的成本節省；若進一步搭配「依時段自動縮放（time-of-day autoscaling）」技術，節省幅度更可達到 25% 以上。不過，Cline 也特別提醒，這種程度的優化通常只適用於每年 AI 算力花費超過 50 萬美元的大型企業。
兼顧價格與資料主權，自建節點將成標配？
基於這份實測數據，Cline 對 AI 基礎設施的未來發展做出了大膽預測。他們認為，隨著企業對人工智慧的採用率不斷攀升、Token 消耗量急劇擴大，「自己託管開放權重模型」將無可避免地成為業界的標準做法。
團隊強調，這不僅僅是為了在價格上取得優勢，更重要的是企業能將敏感的數據保留在自家伺服器內，從而掌握完整的「資料主權（data sovereignty）」。Cline 表示，Kimi K3 模型的推出讓這個未來願景更進了一步，為市場提供了更廣泛且更具競爭力的選擇。
社群打臉：若看「每任務成本」Kimi 反而更貴
儘管 Cline 的實測展現了自託管架構的潛力，但這份報告卻在社群中引發了不同的聲浪。部分開發者認為，單純比較 Token 價格並不能真實反映 AI 模型在實際應用中的性價比。
知名社群使用者 @morganlinton 就在貼文下方犀利回覆指出：「如果看每任務成本（cost per task），Kimi K3 其實比 Fable 5 更貴，我們不能只看輸入與輸出代幣的價格。」他進一步舉例說明，同樣是完成一項特定的任務，Fable 5 可能只需花費 12.18 美元，但使用 Kimi K3 卻得耗費 27.43 美元。
這番見解點出了一個關鍵盲點：當模型的推理邏輯與指令遵循能力較弱時，往往需要消耗更多的 Token 反覆嘗試，這使得 Kimi K3 在某些複雜場景中，反而成為一個相對昂貴的模型。這場關於算力成本的論戰，也突顯了企業在評估 AI 解決方案時，必須在單價與實際任務效率之間取得微妙平衡。

title: Galaxy Digital 推出「比特幣量子就緒計劃」，砸 500 萬鎂資助後量子密碼開發
summary:
面對未來量子運算（Quantum Computing）可能帶來的破壞性威脅，加密金融巨頭 Galaxy Dig […]

〈Galaxy Digital 推出「比特幣量子就緒計劃」，砸 500 萬鎂資助後量子密碼開發〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
面對未來量子運算（Quantum Computing）可能帶來的破壞性威脅，加密金融巨頭 Galaxy Digital 正式打響比特幣安全防衛戰的第一槍。據 Galaxy 於 7 月 21 日發布的官方公告，該公司宣布推出「比特幣量子就緒計劃」（Bitcoin Quantum Readiness Initiative），承諾提供高達 500 萬美元的開發者資助金、成立權威的量子諮詢委員會，並呼籲全產業共同關注與升級比特幣的後量子密碼學防線。
（前情提要：特朗普白宮簽署「量子突進」行政令，公開稱讚IBM CEO，股價盤前飆3%）
（背景補充：G7 央行首發報告：量子電腦 10 年內破解現代密碼！警告「先收割後解密」系統性危機）
為了保護價值數千億美元的去中心化資產，全球加密貨幣產業必須開始與時間賽跑。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 21 日，數位資產與區塊鏈金融巨頭 Galaxy Digital 發布官方新聞稿，宣布啟動「Galaxy 比特幣量子就緒計劃」（Galaxy Bitcoin Quantum Readiness Initiative），希望透過資金支援、權威研究與專家指導，為比特幣網路建立應對量子電腦攻擊的防禦體系。
量子時間表壓縮，比特幣密碼學面臨考驗
比特幣網路的安全根基，主要依賴於「橢圓曲線密碼學」（ECC）。然而，隨著量子運算的快速進步，理論上足夠強大的量子電腦（例如運用 Shor 演算法）將具備破解傳統密碼學的能力。儘管目前具備密碼學破解意義的量子電腦尚未問世，但威脅出現的時間表正在大幅縮短。
美國國家標準與技術研究院（NIST）已於 2024 年發布首批後量子密碼學（PQC）標準，且美國政府也頒布行政命令，要求聯邦系統必須在 2031 年前全面防禦量子攻擊。Galaxy 特別指出，由於比特幣採用去中心化治理，一項協議升級從設計、審核、測試到全網節點部署，往往需要數年時間。然而目前專注於比特幣量子韌性開發的工程師數量極為有限，與其潛在的風險規模完全不成比例。
三大支柱築防線！提供 500 萬美元開發者資助
為了扭轉這項劣勢，Galaxy 推出的量子就緒計劃將由三大核心支柱組成：
- 開發者資助計畫（Developer Grant Program）：Galaxy 承諾提供最高 500 萬美元的資金，用以資助致力於後量子密碼學解決方案的研究者與開發者。優先支持領域包含：抗量子交易提案的實作與審核、後量子簽名方案在比特幣中的整合、錢包與託管遷移工具，以及正式的安全審計等。資助即日起開放申請，並採取里程碑撥款機制。
- 研究與出版計劃（Research and Publishing Program）：由 Galaxy Research 團隊持續發布有關量子威脅與防禦進展的深度報告，為機構投資人、政策制定者及社群提供嚴謹且易懂的資訊。
- 量子諮詢委員會（Quantum Advisory Council）：邀請全球量子計算與後量子密碼學領域的頂尖專家組成，負責指導研究方向與評估開發者提案。首屆成員包含卡爾加里大學量子城市科學主任 Barry Sanders、MIT 專家 Damien Bérubé 以及波士頓大學電腦科學教授 Eran Tromer。
Novogratz：我們有責任保護比特幣長遠安全
對於這項具前瞻性的戰略佈局，Galaxy 創辦人兼執行長麥克·諾沃格拉茨（Mike Novogratz）表示：「作為數位資產領域的領航者，我們認為有責任參與解決量子計算對比特幣的潛在威脅。這項計劃反映了我們的承諾，透過研究、資助與生態支持，確保比特幣的長期安全。」
Galaxy 研究主管 Alex Thorn 也補充說明，量子計算技術發展迅猛，但比特幣開發社群才剛開始認真面對後量子時代的到來。Galaxy 希望扮演橋樑的角色，一方面讓市場理解威脅所在，另一方面為最艱難的底層技術工程提供資金來源。
諮詢委員會專家 Barry Sanders 則強調，全球政府與傳統金融產業都已經在為量子時代做準備，比特幣自然不能例外。Galaxy 號召產業內的機構、開發者與研究團隊共同響應，攜手構建能夠抵禦未來威脅的後量子加密防線。

title: 交易員 jasonleo 用 300 比特幣建倉、現已落袋 6,000 萬鎂！上一輪 1.2 億美元獲利歸零，本輪目標 3 億鎂
summary:
據交易員 jasonleo 於 X（前 Twitter）發布的最新貼文，他分享了自己在比特幣交易中的最新部位與 […]

〈交易員 jasonleo 用 300 比特幣建倉、現已落袋 6,000 萬鎂！上一輪 1.2 億美元獲利歸零，本輪目標 3 億鎂〉這篇文章最早發佈於動區BlockTempo《動區動趨-最具影響力的區塊鏈新聞媒體》。
full_text:
據交易員 jasonleo 於 X（前 Twitter）發布的最新貼文，他分享了自己在比特幣交易中的最新部位與風控心法。他透露，在上一輪交易中雖然曾達到 1.2 億美元的浮盈，但最終因判斷錯誤導致利潤全數回吐；在汲取教訓後，本輪他以 300 枚比特幣建倉，目前已實現 6,000 萬美元盈利，並強調寧可踏空也絕不接受被一波帶走的風險。
（前情提要：Michael Saylor 二度砲轟 BIP-110 軟分叉：比特幣要的是中立不是「貨幣純度」）
（背景補充：比特幣衝 65,800 美元刷新兩週新高！低波動率處於歷史「三次崩盤前」區間）
在波動劇烈的加密貨幣市場中，即便擁有過億美元的浮動利潤，若缺乏嚴格的風險控制，也可能在一夜之間歸零。台北時間 2026 年 7 月 21 日，社群知名交易員 jasonleo（@Jason60704294）發文分享其最新的建倉歷程與交易紀律，吸引了大量加密貨幣社群的關注與討論。
上一轮150BTC建仓，目标1.5亿美金。最高已实现盈利1.2亿美金，最后关头，在12万下跌这里预判错方向，盈利全部抹平，最后保住了本金，以及略微盈利一点。
本轮300BTC建仓，目标3亿美金。 目前已实现盈利6000万— jasonleo (@Jason60704294) July 21, 2026
上輪 1.2 億美金浮盈全抹平！12 萬美元關卡判斷失誤
jasonleo 在貼文中檢討了上一輪的建倉經驗。他表示，自己在上一輪交易中投入了 150 枚比特幣（BTC）作為建倉資金，目標是達到 1.5 億美元的盈利。在行情高漲時期，其持倉的最高盈利一度達到 1.2 億美元。
然而，行情並未一帆風順。在比特幣價格回落至 12 萬美元附近時，他承認自己在最後關頭預判錯了市場方向，導致先前累積的 1.2 億美元盈利全數抹平。所幸在最終平倉時，他及時保住了初始本金，最終僅獲得微幅的利潤出場。
本輪 300BTC 重招！目標 3 億鎂，已落袋 6,000 萬美元
在結束上一輪的波折後，jasonleo 調整策略並重新出發。他透露，本輪交易他加碼至 300 枚比特幣建倉，將整體獲利目標設定為 3 億美元。截至發文時，該筆操作狀況良好，目前已經成功落袋約 6,000 萬美元的已實現盈利。
面對上一次利潤回吐的教訓，他在補充貼文中強調了交易習慣與風控體系的重要性。jasonleo 寫道：「規則不斷建立，習慣不斷形成。在上一輪盈利全部抹平的教訓中，嚴格吸取了風控紀律等習慣。」
他進一步總結自己的核心交易心法，指出在合約或高槓桿交易的世界裡，投資人可以看錯行情、也可以錯失行情而「踏空」，但絕不能允許自己缺乏止損機制。「可以踏空，可以看錯，但是拒絕任何被一波帶走的概率，」jasonleo 寫道。

title: 2026 世足預測市場全紀錄：4.7 億美元押注背後，有人兩場豪賺 825 萬美元
summary:
世界盃冠軍出爐，但預測市場的輸贏才剛揭曉。4.7 億美元押注、近 3,000 萬美元總獲利背後，有人靠兩場比賽翻身賺 825 萬美元，也有人豪擲千萬美元落敗。鏈上數據揭開巨鯨下注背後的真相。

〈2026 世足預測市場全紀錄：4.7 億美元押注背後，有人兩場豪賺 825 萬美元〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
作者：Frank，PANews
7 月 20 日，美加墨世界盃終於落幕，這場吸引全球億萬球迷的盛事不僅在場內引發了巨大關注，在場外也牽動著無數投機者的錢包，此前，PA Beacon 曾統計過小組賽階段的聰明錢預測結果，在世界盃開賽初期，預測市場裡的大額資金並沒有表現出明顯優勢。 PA Beacon 在 2026 年 6 月 17 日統計前 20 場比賽時，賽前買入金額為 8954.57 萬美元，金額命中率只有 48.5%；按持有至結算估算，整體虧損 175.94 萬美元，ROI 為-2.0% 。
一個月後，結果改變了。世界盃全部 104 場比賽結束後，PA Beacon 統計到 4.7404 億美元賽前買入，其中 2.9849 億美元押對方向，金額命中率升至 62.97% 。如果把這些部位都以買進後持有至結算計算，總回款約 5.0293 億美元，估算淨利 2,888.58 萬美元，ROI 為 6.09% 。
從虧損到獲利，看起來像是大額資金在賽程推進中逐漸找回了判斷力。但拆到帳戶層面後，答案沒有這麼簡單：少數錢包只靠一兩場重倉，就拿走了大部分利潤；另一些帳戶幾乎押遍整屆世界杯，命中率更高，最終收益卻相對有限。利潤榜與能力榜，並非同一張榜單。
本文統計口徑：樣本涵蓋 104 場比賽、 312 勝負與平手盤口。交易來自 Polymarket Data API，預篩選條件為單筆金額不低於 5000 美元，只統計開賽前 BUY 交易；同一錢包在同一比賽、同一盤口和同一方向的多筆買入合併計算。盈虧以持有至結算估算，未納入中途賣出、賽中交易、其他盤口對沖和費用，因此不等同於帳戶真實最終盈虧。
大額資金完成翻盤，但利潤集中在少數帳戶
在統計的 1856 個參與賽前買進的錢包中，有 1003 個以上述口徑估算獲利，853 個虧損，獲利錢包佔 54.04% 。獲利帳戶合計賺 9,963.38 萬美元，虧損帳戶合計虧損 7,074.80 萬美元，抵銷後這些聰明錢合計完成 2,888.58 萬美元淨利。
更值得注意的是利潤的集中度。獲利前 5 名帳戶合計賺取 3,770.64 萬美元，佔全部獲利錢包毛利的 37.85%；前 10 名合計賺取 5,518.69 萬美元，佔比達 55.39% 。換句話說，全市場 6.09% 的獲利預期，並不代表大多數大額資金都獲得了穩定優勢，而是少數重倉贏家明顯提高了平均成績。
此外，比賽之間的差異同樣很大。比利時對埃及吸引了 1239.05 萬美元賽前買入，但只有 66.70 萬美元押對，金額命中率僅 5.4%；比利時對塞內加爾的賽前買入金額為 1204.38 萬美元，其中 1053.26 萬美元押對，命中率達到 87.5% 。相近的資金規模，結果完全不同。大額並不等於正確，決定收益的仍是買入方向、賠率和部位。
一兩場重倉，製造了最顯眼的贏家
帳號「mintblade」是最典型的案例。這個帳戶只參與了 2 場比賽、 3 個聚合部位，投入 728.89 萬美元，估算獲利 825.35 萬美元，ROI 達到 113.23%，金額命中率為 100% 。其中，伊朗對紐西蘭一場比賽貢獻了 677.38 萬美元利潤，佔其世界盃估算利潤的 82.1% 。
他的交易的邏輯並不複雜。「mintblade」以 647.05 萬美元買入「伊朗不勝」，平均價格約 0.49 美元。最終雙方 2 比 2 平，該部位以 1 美元結算，估算回款 1324.43 萬美元。隨後，他又在沙烏地阿拉伯對烏拉圭一戰買進「烏拉圭不勝」和少量平手份額，兩筆合計再賺約 147.97 萬美元。兩場比賽全部押對，讓他進入本屆世界盃最賺錢的帳戶之列。但其為何能夠如此大膽的在這兩場比賽下重註卻是耐人尋味。
相較之下，帳號名稱「GRIMDRIP」的地址則更加誇張。他只參與捷克對南非一場比賽，同時買入「捷克不勝」和「比賽平手」兩個相關方向。最終比數為 1 比 1，兩個部位都正確，584.90 萬美元投入帶來 744.97 萬美元估算利潤，ROI 為 127.37% 。
在這些大額下注的背後，是對比賽結果篤定的態度，令人猜測這類地址的大額盈利似乎存在不為人知的秘密。
另一個帳戶「DEEDDIT」則代表另一種重倉方式。他涵蓋 8 場比賽、 9 個聚合部位，投入 2,094.93 萬美元，估算獲利 806.36 萬美元。 32 強比利時 3 比 2 擊敗塞內加爾，他在比利時勝盤口投入 716.10 萬美元，單筆估算賺取 774.95 萬美元；半決賽法國 0 比 2 負於西班牙，他買入「法國不勝」，再賺 342.59 萬美元。
不過，「DEEDDIT」並不是一路正確。他在墨西哥對厄瓜多爾、瑞士對哥倫比亞等比賽中買錯平局方向，幾筆主要虧損超過 430 萬美元。最大一筆獲利相當於其世界盃淨利的 96.1% 。最終排名很高，但高度依賴比利時對塞內加爾這場比賽。
帳戶「sparklingwater123」和「endlessFate」也有相似特徵。前者只涵蓋 2 場比賽，投入 850.05 萬美元，估算獲利 774.69 萬美元；後者覆蓋 5 場，投入 1144.54 萬美元，估算獲利 619.29 萬美元。他們多次在熱門隊直接取勝的價格過高時買入「不勝」或平局，但並非機械地反對熱門，而是在少數比賽中集中表達判斷。整體來看，這類巨鯨的操作可能存在多個平台對沖或差價套利。
「賭徒」豪擲 1599 萬參與 97 場預測，收益不如別人 2 場零頭
如果只看利潤榜，帳號「swisstony」並不突出，但論參與的場次頻率，他絕對是王者。他的預測涵蓋 97 場比賽、 267 個聚合部位，賽前買進 1599.12 萬美元，金額命中率達 79.29%，估算獲利 124.82 萬美元，ROI 為 7.81% 。不過，他押中的比賽雖遠多於「mintblade」和「GRIMDRIP」，盈利只有前者的約 15% 。
差異主要來自部位結構。「swisstony」單筆最大估算獲利只有 22.27 萬美元，最大虧損為 30.58 萬美元，最大獲利部位只佔其世界盃淨利的 17.84% 。他沒有依賴某一場比賽完成翻盤，而是在大量比賽中用更小的部位累積收益。這樣的結果不夠戲劇化，卻更能說明一個帳戶是否具備持續優勢。
帳號「AV23IUa」和「Latina」也屬於覆蓋範圍相對更廣的獲利帳戶。「AV23IUa」參與 46 場、 46 個部位，投入 212.45 萬美元，估算獲利 90.60 萬美元，ROI 為 42.65%；「Latina」覆蓋 11 場，投入 342.93 萬美元，估算獲利 129.20 萬美元，金額命中率為 88.64% 。兩者的利潤都沒有集中在單一比賽上。
另一個值得注意的帳戶是「zhqzhq」。以每場正確方向資金是否超過一半的口徑，他涵蓋的 14 場比賽全部判斷正確，但 101.82 萬美元投入只帶來 5.57 萬美元估算利潤，ROI 為 5.47% 。命中率很高，但收益不高，原因是他買的時候往往比賽已經處於高度確定性階段。
贏家之外，虧損帳戶提供了更直接的對照。「LEEEROYJENKINS」在澳洲對土耳其一場估算獲利 479.76 萬美元，但隨後重倉比利時戰勝埃及，比賽最終 1 比 1，單場估算虧損 839.43 萬美元。先前的大額獲利被一次錯誤抵消，其世界盃旅程最終估算虧損 324.64 萬美元。
而更多的虧損玩家則以連續壓錯為主。帳號「coldsway」投入 1372.55 萬美元，涵蓋 9 場比賽，金額命中率只有 26.22%，最終估算虧損 734.37 萬美元，是帳戶層面的最大輸家。帳號「FlickRaw」只參與 2 場，兩場都判斷錯誤，479.83 萬美元投入全部歸零。
這些案例說明，這些巨鯨的底色仍然是一擲千金的賭客。一次過重的錯誤部位，足以抵銷先前多次正確。
巨鯨眼中的奪冠熱門：法國被嚴重高估，西班牙最穩
比賽進入末段，四強的球隊，法國、英格蘭、阿根廷、西班牙作為奪冠最熱門的四支隊伍一直備受關注，大筆資金對他們的預測，也更能體現巨鯨們的真實實力。
西班牙：西班牙是四隊中資金判斷最穩定的樣本。五場淘汰賽裡，金額較大的一側全部押對。但支持強度並非一路上升：32 強至四分之一決賽，支持西班牙獲勝的資金從 114.3 萬美元升至 239.0 萬美元；而在半決賽對法國卻降至 87.9 萬美元，買入成本中位數只有 0.297 美元。最後西班牙以 2 比 0 勝，這反而成了賠率空間最大的一場。不過，這 87.9 萬美元並不是廣泛共識，最大帳戶貢獻 46.7%，前五名帳戶佔 73.5% 。五場全中，說明少數重倉資金連續站對了方向，但整體市場卻判斷錯誤了。
阿根廷：阿根廷的曲線相反。雖然球隊一路逆襲，進入決賽。但直接支持資金卻逐漸滑坡。 32 強支援金額 280.4 萬美元、成本中位數 0.86 美元，四強已降至 39.3 萬美元和 0.315 美元。決賽前，支持阿根廷獲勝的資金只有 43.4 萬美元，反對資金達 151.8 萬美元，支持佔 22.2% 。這一次，資金提前轉向「不勝」並判斷正確。不過，前五個反對帳戶佔該側資金 92.5%，最大帳戶單獨佔 44.4%，仍是少數大戶主導的結論。
法國：法國呈現最明顯的「少數正確、群體錯誤」。準決賽對西班牙，支持法國獲勝的資金為 162.6 萬美元，反對資金達到 719.4 萬美元，最終大資金獲勝，但資金構成主要來自單一錢包貢獻約 576 萬美元，佔反對資金 80.1% 。到了三、四名決賽，資金又大幅轉向法國：299.97 萬美元支持法國取勝，17.93 萬美元反對，支持佔 94.4% 。結果法國 4 比 6 不敵英格蘭。
英格蘭：英格蘭則是最容易被低估的球隊。 16 強對墨西哥，支持英格蘭的資金為 114.4 萬美元，反對資金為 118.7 萬美元，金額共識站在「不勝」一側，英格蘭卻 3 比 2 晉級。三、四名決賽對法國，支持英格蘭的資金只有 15.9 萬美元，反對資金達到 103.2 萬美元，支持佔比僅 13.4%，買入成本中位數只有 0.210 美元，最終英格蘭 6 比 4 取勝。但這兩場都不是「聰明錢集體看錯」：三四名賽反對英格蘭的前五大帳戶佔該側資金 98.3%，其中最大帳戶佔 60.4%，是少數重倉帳戶把金額共識拉向了錯誤方向。
當美加墨世界盃的喧囂散去，這場持續 40 天的「預測狂歡」也畫上了句號。複盤這些鏈上數據，我們看到了一個無比真實又殘酷的投機世界：在這裡，資金規模並不等同於先知先覺，「聰明錢」也會被群體偏見反噬；在這裡，有人靠一兩場冷門一夜暴富，也有人機關算盡卻敵不過一次重倉失誤。
撥開「倖存者偏差」的迷霧，那些最顯眼的獲利神話，底色依然是驚心動魄的豪賭。足球場上沒有永遠的常勝將軍，投機市場亦然。

title: MetaMask 開發商遭北韓滲透！外部顧問潛伏近一個月，官方證實展開調查
summary:
開發商 Consensys 遭北韓人員化名滲透，接觸 MetaMask 程式碼近一個月。官方確認無資產受損，已撤銷權限並展開全面調查。

〈MetaMask 開發商遭北韓滲透！外部顧問潛伏近一個月，官方證實展開調查〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
作者：Kurumi，加密城市
北韓相關承包商滲入 Consensys，MetaMask 程式碼開放近一個月
以太坊基礎建設公司 Consensys 捲入資安風暴。根據《Drop Site》的報導，該公司今年稍早透過一家具信譽的第三方服務供應商，引入一名使用「Tyler Knapp」化名的軟體開發顧問，該人士後續被查出與北韓有關。此人曾參與 MetaMask 相關開發工作，並於 3 月 9 日至 4 月期間接觸部分系統與程式碼，直到 Consensys 發現異常後終止其權限。
Consensys 法務長 Matt Corva 向外媒《Cointelegraph》表示，該名開發者從未成為公司正式員工，身分是外部顧問。公司確認威脅後，已依內部資安流程撤銷其存取權限，並啟動全面調查。
調查結果顯示，目前沒有發現資產或資料遭挪用，也沒有惡意程式碼被部署，使用者安全與錢包資產未受影響。公司同時通報執法機關，並重新檢視外包工程與第三方服務管理流程。
內部警報暫停產品發佈，第三方用工漏洞浮上檯面
事件曝光後，外界關注焦點集中在 MetaMask 程式碼與產品發佈流程。據報導，Consensys 曾於 4 月發佈內部警示，要求暫停所有產品版本發佈，直到調查完成為止，並提醒員工停止與該名顧問互動。對一家管理全球大量鏈上使用者入口的錢包公司而言，這類措施顯示管理層當時已將事件視為高風險資安事件處理。
這起事件也凸顯加密產業對外包工程人力的依賴風險。許多開源或半開源專案需要與外部開發者、承包商、審計公司與服務商合作，權限控管若未細緻分級，具備合法帳號的外部人員便可能接觸敏感儲存庫、提交程式碼或取得內部開發資訊。即使調查未發現實際損害，外部顧問能持續接觸 MetaMask 相關程式碼近一個月，已足以引發錢包安全與供應鏈治理疑慮。
北韓 IT 滲透加密業，攻擊已從釣魚轉向供應鏈
北韓相關駭客與 IT 工作者近年持續鎖定加密貨幣產業。美國執法與資安單位多次警告，北韓人員會以假身分、偽造履歷、遠端工作設備與第三方承包關係，進入科技公司與加密企業內部，藉此取得程式碼、雲端憑證、私鑰管理資訊或內部系統權限。這類攻擊路徑比單純釣魚更隱蔽，因為入侵者可透過正式流程取得帳號，並在日常開發活動中降低被發現機率。
MetaMask 是全球最常用的自託管錢包之一，長期作為使用者進入 DeFi 、 NFT 與鏈上應用的主要入口。即便 Consensys 強調使用者資產安全未受影響，事件仍讓市場重新檢視錢包開發流程的脆弱環節。
- 對使用者而言，錢包前端、瀏覽器擴充功能、簽章提示與交易確認介面，都可能在供應鏈環節遭遇風險。
- 對企業而言，身分驗證、最小權限、程式碼審查、版本凍結與異常存取監控，已成為加密基礎設施維運的核心要求。
Consensys 承諾強化審查，加密錢包安全壓力升高
Consensys 表示，將重新評估外包工程與第三方服務商合作規範，讓外部關係適用更嚴格的審查標準。未來承包商是否完成身分驗證、是否接受多輪面試、是否使用硬體驗證、是否限制地理位置與 IP 存取、是否能接觸關鍵儲存庫，都可能成為錢包公司風控制度的一部分。
這起事件沒有造成已知資產損失，卻讓加密產業看見另一種高強度攻擊模式。攻擊者取得開發流程中的合法位置後，風險會向產品發佈、程式碼完整性與使用者信任擴散。對 MetaMask 這類基礎入口而言，安全問題已超越單一漏洞修補，延伸至人員、供應商、權限與治理流程的全面防線。
（以上內容獲合作夥伴《加密城市》授權節錄及轉載，原文連結 ）

title: 部署者爽領 50% 手續費！Hyperliquid 將開放「無許可」創建預測市場
summary:
去中心化永續合約交易平台 Hyperliquid 加速布局預測市場，宣布將進一步升級 HIP-4，讓任何人都能在平台上部署預測市場合約，正式向目前由 Polymarket 與 Kalshi 主導的市場發起挑戰。

〈部署者爽領 50% 手續費！Hyperliquid 將開放「無許可」創建預測市場〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
去中心化永續合約交易平台 Hyperliquid 加速布局預測市場，宣布將進一步升級 HIP-4，讓任何人都能在平台上部署預測市場合約，正式向目前由 Polymarket 與 Kalshi 主導的市場發起挑戰。
Hyperliquid 透過 Telegram 表示，HIP-4 導入的「Outcome Trading（結果交易）」功能，未來只要採用經驗證者投票通過的標準化範本，任何人都能自由建置預測市場合約。在新功能全面開放前，現有預測市場仍由驗證者負責建立與管理。
預測市場成新戰場，Hyperliquid 加入競爭
預測市場是近年區塊鏈產業成長最快的領域，允許用戶針對特定事件結果進行交易，例如央行利率決策、總統大選和體育賽事等，透過市場價格反映事件發生機率。
目前全球預測市場主要由 Polymarket 與 Kalshi 主導，市場規模已突破數十億美元。
隨著需求快速成長，愈來愈多大型金融平台也開始加入競爭。今年剛落幕的 2026 FIFA 世足賽，預測市場累計交易金額更突破 500 億美元，吸引包括 Coinbase 、 Robinhood 等中心化交易平台相繼布局，希望提供涵蓋預測市場與傳統金融商品的一站式交易服務。
開放任何人建立預測市場，但需質押 50 萬枚 HYPE
HIP-4 已於今年 5 月正式部署至 Hyperliquid 主網，目前平台已支援「結果交易」功能。
Hyperliquid 表示，未來首先會在測試網開放無許可預測市場，確認運作穩定後，再推向主網。
屆時，任何人都能部署自己的預測市場，但必須先質押 50 萬枚 HYPE（Hyperliquid 原生代幣）作為保證金。
若驗證者投票認定市場定義不清、規則設計存在重大瑕疵，或最終結算結果錯誤，這筆質押資產可能遭到削減（Slashing，指沒收部分質押資產作為懲罰）。
作為回報，建立預測市場的開發者最高可獲得 50% 的交易手續費收入，藉此鼓勵社群持續建立更多高品質市場。
Hyperliquid 表示，未來開放無許可預測市場後，目前由驗證者建立的官方市場仍會繼續存在，但數量將大幅減少。
官方指出，理想情況下，每年由驗證者建立的市場將少於 10 個，大部分市場將交由社群自主建立與維護。
HYPE 小幅走揚
消息公布後，市場反應偏向正面。 Hyperliquid 原生代幣 HYPE 在公告發布後一度上漲約 1%，自盤中低點 59.88 美元回升至 60.5 美元以上，最新報價約 62.55 美元，過去 24 小時上漲 3.3% 。
隨著預測市場持續成為加密貨幣產業競逐的新焦點，Hyperliquid 這次升級也意味著業務版圖正從去中心化衍生品交易，進一步延伸至預測市場，與 Polymarket 、 Kalshi 等平台展開正面競爭。

title: 川普點頭接受「道德條款」！美國《CLARITY 法案》闖關參院再進一步
summary:
美國加密貨幣監管立法再傳重大進展。美國總統川普（Donald Trump）已同意納入備受爭議的「道德條款」，為《數位資產市場明晰法案（CLARITY 法案）》掃除最後一道主要障礙，也讓這部攸關美國加密貨幣監管架構的法案，更接近在參議院完成表決。

〈川普點頭接受「道德條款」！美國《CLARITY 法案》闖關參院再進一步〉這篇文章最早發佈於《區塊客》。
full_text:
美國加密貨幣監管立法再傳重大進展。美國總統川普（Donald Trump）已同意納入備受爭議的「道德條款」，為《數位資產市場明晰法案（CLARITY 法案）》掃除最後一道主要障礙，也讓這部攸關美國加密貨幣監管架構的法案，更接近在參議院完成表決。
業內知情人士向外媒《The Block》透露，經過長達數月的馬拉松式協商，各方終於在道德條款上取得共識：「我們最新掌握的消息是，川普已經接受了這項條款。」
上述消息最初由《Crypto in America》記者 Eleanor Terrett 與《Punchbowl News》記者 Brendan Pedersen 率先披露。不過 Brendan Pedersen 也補充，民主黨陣營目前尚未看到該條款的最終文本。
回顧 7 月 16 日，川普曾與共和黨籍參議員 Bernie Moreno 、 Cynthia Lummis 以及白宮加密貨幣顧問 Patrick Witt 召開閉門會議，專門探討這項條款。儘管當時並未達成共識，但川普最終於周一晚間簽字同意。針對消息，白宮及兩位參議員辦公室尚未做出回應。
化解利益衝突爭議，《CLARITY 法案》迎來曙光
《CLARITY 法案》將首度在聯邦層級建立完整的加密貨幣監管制度，並明確劃分美國證管會（SEC）、美國商品期貨交易委員會（CFTC）的監管權責，被視為美國加密產業最重要的監管法案，而「道德規範」也一直是推動這部法案的主要障礙。
據《Politico》報導，在上周會議前，部分民主黨人對遞交給總統的道德條款版本仍持反對意見。過去一年來，國會與白宮針對該條款爭論不休，核心目的在於防弊，嚴格限制總統、副總統、國會議員及其他聯邦高階官員，在任期間透過數位資產獲利。
這場利益衝突的暴風眼，則是圍繞川普發行的迷因幣，以及其家族主導的 DeFi 項目 World Liberty Financial（WLF）。根據上個月公布的財務申報資料，川普從 WLF 相關業務中獲得高達數百萬美元的收益，瞬間引爆政界對建立道德規範的激烈論戰。
參院須趕在 8 月初表決
展望後續進程，《CLARITY 法案》的完整條文預計將於近日出爐，隨後交由參議院進行全院表決。於國會時程有限，參議院必須在 8 月第一周前完成表決；若順利通過，法案仍須送回眾議院覆議，之後才會送交川普簽署成為法律。
另一位熟悉協商的人士透露，法案文本最快可能在周一晚間出爐，但也不排除會延後幾天。不過，他認為，公布時間愈晚，代表兩黨持續協商的空間愈大，最終法案獲得跨黨派支持的機率也就愈高。
主導本次立法協商的白宮加密貨幣政策顧問 Patrick Witt，原訂本周因喬治亞州國民兵（Georgia Army National Guard）義務訓練而離職，但他周一在 X 發文表示，相關訓練已延期，因此將繼續留任緊盯法案進度。

title: Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
summary: Joshua Kerry, 28, attacked Widdecombe while she was eating lunch at her home in Devon before stealing her wallet, prosecutors say.
full_text:
Ann Widdecombe was hit on head 21 times with hammer, prosecutors say
- Published
Ann Widdecombe was hit on the head with a hammer 21 times at her home as she ate lunch in an attack that was caught on camera, prosecutors have told Westminster Magistrates' Court.
Prosecutor Kashif Malik said the man charged with her murder, Joshua Kerry, arrived at her house on 8 July in a red Vauxhall Corsa and entered through the front door.
Kerry, who prosecutors say was in the property for two minutes and was wearing black gloves, then allegedly hit Widdecombe repeatedly with a hammer in her kitchen, tipped her from her chair and took her wallet before driving off.
The 28-year-old from South Yorkshire later also appeared at the Old Bailey and was remanded in custody.
At the Old Bailey hearing, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the attack on Widdecombe had been carried out with a "ferocity of violence".
Malik told the court that Widdecombe did not attend a pre-arranged online interview with Channel 5's Matt Allwright show that had been scheduled for just before 13:00 BST on 8 July.
The show's production team tried to contact Widdecombe through her personal assistant, who then asked Widdecombe's gardener to check on her, the court heard.
Prosecutors said the gardener entered the house via the open front door on 9 July and found Widdecombe lying face down on her kitchen floor with a serious head injury.
Malik told the chief magistrate that security camera footage from her home in Haytor, Devon, showed she had been fatally attacked the day before.
He added that police were still investigating whether there was a terrorism connection or political motivation for the attack.
Kerry, from Rotherham, was charged with one count of murder on Monday night following an investigation led by counter-terrorism detectives.
He appeared emotionless in the dock and spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during the short hearing at Westminster Magistrates' Court. He was not asked to indicate a plea.
Later on Tuesday, he also appeared at the Old Bailey. It is expected that he will be remanded at HMP Belmarsh in south-east London.
He will next appear at the same court on 9 October for a case management hearing.
A provisional trial date has been listed for 8 June 2027.
The court heard that a pathologist had given a provisional cause of Widdecombe's death as a blunt force injury to the head.
An earlier inquest hearing, that was opened and adjourned on Tuesday, heard that emergency services were called on the day Widdecombe was found, but she was pronounced dead at 12:20.
The hearing was also told that while a post-mortem examination had taken place, "at this stage the precise medical cause of death has yet to be established".
Widdecombe's career in politics spanned decades.
She served as Conservative MP for Maidstone in Kent for 23 years and was appointed to ministerial roles in Sir John Major's government in the 1990s.
Following her departure from the Commons, Widdecombe appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing in 2010 and was a runner-up on Celebrity Big Brother eight years later.
She later represented South West England as a Member of the European Parliament (MEP) for the Brexit Party and in 2023 she joined Reform UK as a party spokeswoman.

title: Burnham tells cabinet to tackle living costs at first meeting
summary: The new prime minister chaired his first cabinet after announcing a cut to VAT on household electricity.
full_text:
Burnham tells cabinet to tackle living costs at first meeting
- Published
Andy Burnham has promised to lead a "cost of living government," as he chaired his first cabinet meeting as prime minister.
He told his newly-assembled top team that he wanted to make living expenses a key priority, and give people a "sense that help is coming" on costs.
It comes after he announced a VAT cut to household energy bills from October, in his first major announcement since taking office.
But his plan to pay for the policy by scrapping Sir Keir Starmer's digital ID scheme led to an early row over whether the plan was properly funded.
Downing Street said the estimated £850m cost of the VAT cut over the rest of the financial year could come from £1.8bn earmarked by the previous government to roll out the digital ID scheme in the next three years.
But Darren Jones, who was among a clutch of Starmer loyalists sacked from the cabinet on Monday, said the ID programme was "unfunded" and Burnham would need to set out where the money would be found.
Opposition parties also seized on the announcement, pointing out the government's budget watchdog has previously said the money to fund digital ID was due to be found from within existing budgets.
"We are only one day in and already Labour are playing fast and loose with the public finances," said Conservative shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride.
The PM's spokesman insisted the policy would be funded by redirecting "savings" identified by departments to cover the cost of the ID scheme.
Burnham was given a round of applause by his senior ministers earlier, as he opened the first meeting of his new cabinet after appointing his top team on Monday evening. More junior picks are expected to follow on Tuesday.
Monday's wide-ranging reshuffle saw Starmer loyalists such as Rachel Reeves and David Lammy out of government, with Ed Miliband promoted to foreign secretary and Burnham ally Louise Haigh given a big job running the Cabinet Office.
In a move that took Westminster by surprise, John Healey, who resigned as Starmer's defence secretary in a row over military spending, has been given the crucial role of chancellor.
Speaking to staff at the Treasury, where he was a minister during the New Labour period, Healey said discipline over tax and spending would be his "first duty", as he recommitted to the tax and spending rules set by his predecessor.
But he added that government would seek to make the "fullest possible use of public investment" within the framework, alongside making the most of private and international investment.
Speaking at the start of the meeting attended by broadcasters, Burnham said the cost of living would be an early priority, with further measures to be announced in the coming days.
He said he would be asking ministers to come up with suggestions to lower costs to households, adding: "There are things can be done, big and small."
He insisted his government would always show "how we are going to pay for" policies, adding "discipline" on spending would be required.
But he conceded that funding new announcements ahead of his first Budget, where big tax decisions are made, would require ministers to be "prepared to reprioritise" how they allocate their budgets.
This was also reflected in Burnham's first announcement on Monday, a further £340m to tackle rough sleeping over five years, which is expected to be funded within "uncommitted" spending at the housing department.
'No 10 North'
The announcement on energy bills, which will see VAT on household electricity reduced from 5% to zero in England, Wales and Scotland, is estimated to save the typical household about £45 a year.
It will not apply in Northern Ireland due to post-Brexit rules agreed by the previous Conservative government, with ministers at Stormont instead offered extra money from the Treasury to use on cost of living measures.
The Conservatives and Reform UK have both previously called for the measure, with Nigel Farage calling it a benefit of Brexit but insisting it would not "address the real issue of the cost of living" and taking aim at green levies on bills.
Meanwhile, further details have been confirmed of Burnham's plan for a new Downing Street unit in Manchester, known as No 10 North.
The government says the unit, expected to be initially set up in a building currently housing intelligence service GCHQ, will be given control of aspects of local economic growth and devolution strategy.
Alongside this, a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet will be created to ensure departments remain focused on "top strategic priorities", according to a statement announcing the changes, external.
Civil servants working in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move north, it is understood, with Downing Street saying Burnham would try to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week".

title: London-based civil servants offered move to No 10 North in Manchester
summary: London-based civil servants willing to move north have been told they will be offered relocation packages, the BBC understands.
full_text:
Whitehall officials offered move to No 10 North in Manchester
- Published
Civil servants working for government departments based in London have been offered relocation packages to encourage them to move to the North of England, the BBC understands.
It comes as the first details are emerging about the new No 10 North, which Downing Street says is already up and running.
The BBC has been told that the Northern branch of Downing Street will be overseen by cabinet minister and ally of Burnham, Louise Haigh.
Haigh, who is the first secretary of state, is thought to have been asked to lead a new Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet (OPMC), which will give her control of key decision-making bodies across government.
The OPMC will include No 10, No 10 North and teams within the Cabinet Office.
Addressing his cabinet for the first time, Burnham said No 10 North was "not a gimmick" and that the "time for resisting devolution was over".
A No 10 spokesman said the prime minister was expecting to work from No 10 North "at least one day a week" subject to government business.
Announcing the changes,, external which will also establish a new AI taskforce, Leader of the House of Lords, Baroness Angela Smith said No 10 North would be a "dominant driver of the UK's economy".
It is understood that the initial location of No 10 North will be Heron House in central Manchester, in the same building which houses offices for the intelligence service GCHQ. Specialist police officers have been seen guarding the building.
It is likely that the longer term base for No 10 North will be at a new government "Digital Campus" which is under construction in the Ancoats area of Manchester. It is not due for completion until 2032.
However, a good indication of what it could look like comes from a new report, released on Tuesday.
The blueprint has been authored, external by the Re:State think tank which Burnham was involved with until he stepped down as mayor of Greater Manchester.
- Burnham's 'Manchesterism' got him to No 10 - but will it work for the UK? - Published4 days ago
 
- Who's in Andy Burnham's cabinet? - Published1 hour ago
 
It sets out a possible recruitment plan that would bring in new hires from across Greater Manchester and the wider North of England.
In total, the report suggests around 300 staff should be employed within 18 months.
It proposes transferring teams from Whitehall departments, including the Treasury, Cabinet Office, and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government – all of which are now being led by ministers who represent constituencies in the North of England.
Successive governments have sought to move more civil servants out of London and last year a target was set to cut the number of roles in the capital by 12,000.
According to the most recent figures, 19.6% of civil servants are based in London and the number has been gradually decreasing for the past four years.
The percentage of senior civil servants based outside of London stands at 13.5% compared to 34.7% in London.
Whitehall officials willing to move to Manchester have been told they will be offered relocation packages, the BBC understands.
It's also likely there will be a significant movement of staff from Burnham's former mayoral team at the Greater Manchester Combined Authority (GMCA).
The BBC has been told that at least three senior figures are understood to have agreed to work at No 10 North. Some GMCA staff expressed surprise at only finding out their colleagues would be moving after seeing them on TV greeting the new prime minister in Downing Street.
No 10 North will lead on a key plank of Burnham's agenda; handing power from Whitehall and Westminster to regions across the country.
It means strategic decisions about devolution and local economic growth will shift out of the Treasury, now led by Chancellor John Healey, and Angela Rayner's Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government - though both departments will have some "remaining functions" in these areas.

title: Argentina's Fernandez defends team after ugly scenes in World Cup final loss to Spain
summary: Midfielder Enzo Fernandez claims Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" in the World Cup.
full_text:
Fernandez defends Argentina as Messi questions remain
- Published
Midfielder Enzo Fernandez has claimed Argentina represented their nation "in the best possible way" during the World Cup, despite ugly scenes during and after their final loss to Spain.
Fernandez was sent off late in normal time for two yellow cards and Spain won 1-0 after extra time on Sunday in New Jersey.
His first booking was for showing dissent towards Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic and Fernandez was later dismissed for catching Pau Cubarsi with a challenge that sent the defender cartwheeling in the air.
But, in a statement on social media, the Chelsea midfielder did not mention the red card and said: "As time goes by, you realise there is something much bigger than just a result.
"For years, this group has represented the team in the best possible way. It teaches that competing isn't just about winning; it's about giving your all for the jersey and never giving up.
"It has been a privilege to be part of a group that always stepped up, competed at the highest level, and defended these colours with pride, humility, and commitment."
- Keeper Martinez may 'step aside' from Argentina - Published4 hours ago
 
- Fifa opens investigation into Argentina post-final trouble - Published21 hours ago
 
Members of the Argentina team and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain players who had begun to celebrate their World Cup success.
Fifa's disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to assess what happened and any player or coach involved could face suspension, while the Argentine Football Association may also be fined.
Nahuel Molina, Leandro Paredes, Thiago Almada and assistant coach Roberto Ayala all appeared to be involved, with Paredes pushing Spain's Eric Garcia by the throat.
Spain's Gavi tried to intervene, but was forced to the ground by Almada, before Paredes pushed Gavi to the turf by putting his hand in the Spaniard's face.
Ayala then looked to be holding Garcia around the throat, before appearing to strike Spain midfielder Dani Olmo.
'Let's forget everything else'
While the match ended with ugly scenes broadcast around the world, questions remain over what happened behind closed doors prior to kick-off.
There has been widespread speculation on social media about what was said in the Argentina dressing room before the game, including whether Lionel Messi informed his team-mates that the final would be his last match for the national side.
It comes after Argentine television company RLC Noticias posted footage appearing to show Messi urging his team-mates to stay calm on their walk to the tunnel - and "forget about everything else".
In the footage, which has not been verified by the BBC, Messi is seen saying: "Let's go, boys, [let's keep] calm people, calm. The main thing is for us to remain calm, boys, that we remain calm.
"Let's just concentrate on playing, nothing else - calm, OK? Forget everything else.
"Let's just play, let's just concentrate on playing. Let's go."
'We must be gracious in defeat'
The actions of the Argentina players on the pitch were heavily criticised by former England internationals.
Ex-England captain Alan Shearer said: "Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone's face. He went for them. There is no place or space for that.
"We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible."
Former England goalkeeper Joe Hart added: "The game's done, they can have absolutely no complaints about what happened. Disgusting behaviour."
Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni attempted to calm the situation down in his post-match interview.
He said: "We are gracious in victory, and we must be gracious in defeat. Today, we are showing that we know how to lose.
"We lost the match, and we accept it, but that doesn't mean we stop living or forget everything we did to get here."
Argentina, the World Cup winners in 1978, 1986 and 2022, won their first seven matches in North America, beating Algeria, Austria, Jordan, Cape Verde, Egypt, Switzerland and England before losing to Spain.
Against Egypt, Argentina were 2-0 down before scoring three late goals to win and in the semi-final with England, the Three Lions led 1-0 until the 85th minute before goals from Fernandez and a Lautaro Martinez header gave them a 2-1 win.
Several media outlets in Argentina have suggested the final could be Scaloni's last in charge and called it the end of an era, with talisman Lionel Messi, in tears at the end, unlikely to play at another World Cup.
"The pain is immense, and this wound will take time to heal. But I also hold onto all the good things," Messi wrote on social media.
However, the team were still greeted by thousands of Argentina fans with an open-top bus parade through the streets of Buenos Aires.
Scaloni and 16 of his 26 players returned to the country and were welcomed by a red carpet and military band at Ezeiza International Airport.
Aston Villa goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez, who made 11 saves during the final, was among the players in Argentina, but Messi was one of those who did not make the trip, instead returning to Miami where he plays club football for Inter Miami.

title: Row escalates in Ukraine over army chief's future
summary: Protesters are demanding Oleksandr Syrskyi be removed and former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov reinstated by Friday.
full_text:
Row escalates in Ukraine over army chief's future
- Published
Protesters in Ukraine have threatened nationwide demonstrations if Mykhailo Fedorov is not reinstated as defence minister, as President Volodymyr Zelensky scrambles to quell outrage over the decision to oust him.
Over the past week, thousands in Kyiv and other cities have taken to the streets to protest against Fedorov's removal and demand the dismissal of Oleksandr Syrskyi, the commander of Ukraine's armed forces.
Army veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi said in a social media post that if Syrskyi is not dismissed by Friday and Federov reinstated, "we will begin an open-ended nationwide protest".
No protests are scheduled before then, and Ukraine is waiting, anxiously, for a resolution. Over the weekend, Ukrainian media reported that Zelensky was consulting ministers and generals in an effort to resolve the crisis.
Amid a welter of rumours, the general staff was forced to deny reports that Gen Syrskyi was about to be – or even had already been – sacked. Another report suggested that Fedorov had refused an offer to return to a different position in government.
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the president's office, urged Ukrainians to remain calm.
"The situation surrounding the latest internal changes has caused strong emotions," he wrote on Tuesday.
With the noisy calls of angry protesters echoing around the tight confines of Ivana Franka Square, within earshot of the presidential palace, Budanov said the government was taking note.
"I understand people who express their position…..The position of society has been heard."
With large numbers of demonstrators directing their anger towards Gen Syrskyi – seen by many as representing outdated Soviet-era military doctrines, Budanov, a former head of military intelligence, warned people "not to hate anyone".
"The enemy is closely monitoring our every internal dispute and is waiting for us to start fighting among ourselves," he wrote.
"The work is under way. There will be results."
On Monday, the beleaguered but usually silent 60-year-old Gen Syrskyi hit back against his critics, publishing a long defence of his record and urging readers not to focus on his widely-reported rivalry with 35-year-old Mykhailo Fedorov.
Despite Zelensky's claim last week that the two men could not even bear to sit in the same room, Syrskyi said it had been a surprise to learn that he had a conflict with the minister.
"I perceived our relationship as a working one," he wrote in an op-ed for the Militarny website.
"If I offended anyone, Mykhailo Albertovych [Fedorov], I'm sorry."
The general said the issues of military contracts, procurement and mobilisation currently being aired in the press and boiled down to pithy slogans on pieces of cardboard carried aloft by protestors were a great deal more complicated than most people realised.
"Decisions on which people's lives depend are not made with slogans," he said. "Real work, not the public drama surrounding it, wins the war."
Like the ousted defence minister, the commander-in-chief avoided directly personal attacks, but the object of much of his criticism was pretty clear.
"Presentations should not turn into self-representations," he wrote, in a thinly veiled swipe at Federov's long, detailed news conference last week.
"Behind each slide there should be a document, a budget and a procedure," the general went on. "Otherwise, instead of a decision the army gets disappointment."
Syrskyi's problem however is that most Ukrainians, especially the younger ones, seem to trust Federov's analysis of what needs to change in order for Ukraine to win the war, not the general's.
More than anyone, Federov is seen by many as driving innovation in the military, gradually improving Ukraine's chances of beating back its numerically superior enemy.
"Right now, the war is changing, so we need new ideas and a new structure," 44-year-old law company employee Tetiana Makarenko told me at one of the protests over the weekend.
"It's often said that a small Soviet army can't defeat a big Soviet army. It's time to change the mindset and start the new type of war."
Federov's six months at the helm in the defence ministry have coincided with a string of military successes for which the minister, not always fairly perhaps, is credited.
"We had this feeling because we saw the changing situation," Makarenko said. "We had the feeling that we can do this."
In his article, Syrskyi hit back at those accusing him of a lack of strategy, or that he had failed to embrace new technology.
"The strangest reproach that I have heard is that I supposedly do not want to fight with drones," he said, pointing out that he had presided over the creation of an unmanned systems force as a separate branch of the military.
But drones, despite being responsible for the lion's share of Russian casualties, were not enough, he argued.
"I cannot transform a million-strong army to drones in two months and say: now we fight like this."
Syrskyi said he was not at war with the defence ministry but with Russia. But while he mounts his defence against a host of critics, speculation has fallen on who Zelensky might choose to replace him.
The candidates include Mykhailo Drapatyi, commander of the Joint Forces, Andriy Bilekskyi, commander of the Third Army Corps, Oleh Apostol, commander of the Airborne Assault Forces and Ihor Obolenskyi, commander of the National Guard Corps.
All have distinguished military records, but crucially all are from a much younger generation of officers. At 46, Biletskyi is the oldest while Apostol and Obolenskyi are both 39.
At just 35, the youngest possible candidate is Brig Gen Denys Prokopenko, another National guard commander, whose "Azov" Regiment, while politically controversial for its alleged far-right connections, achieved near mythic status during the bitter siege of the southern port city of Mariupol in 2022.
Held as a prisoner of war by Russia following the collapse of the city, Prokopenko returned to Ukraine as part of a prisoner exchange in July 2023, quickly resuming his command despite Russian demands that he remain outside the country until the war was over.
Zelensky says he is still working out "what adjustments need to be made to Ukraine's defence strategy" and has thanked everyone "for their openness, honesty and substantive contributions".
With Russia expected to resume its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure this autumn, the president says "Ukraine must enter August as strong as possible".
As the protests fall silent for now, the country waits for the president to make a series of possibly fateful decisions.

title: Brazil's Amazon sees sharp decline in size of area burned in 2025
summary: The amount of land burned in the world's largest rainforest was the smallest since MapBiomas records began in 1985.
full_text:
Brazil's Amazon sees sharp decline in size of area burned in 2025
- Published
The area burned in Brazil's Amazon in 2025 was far smaller in size than the previous year, according to the deforestation monitoring group MapBiomas.
A MapBiomas report states that 3.1 million hectares of Brazil's Amazon were burned last year, compared with a record-breaking 15.8 million hectares in 2024.
The amount of land burned in the world's largest rainforest last year covered the smallest area since MapBiomas records began in 1985.
Protecting the Amazon was one of the pledges President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made when he was running for running for office four years ago. These latest figures will be seen as a boost to his campaign for re-election in October.
In 2024, the Amazon rainforest experienced its worst forest fires in over two decades, which the Copernicus Climate Change Service put down to "climate extremes and human activity".
"The 2025 figures are significant and show that it is possible to reduce the burned area in the country," Vera Arruda, a researcher at the Amazon Environmental Research Institute (IPAM) and co-ordinator at MapBiomas, told the BBC.
"The 31% drop compared to the historical average - driven primarily by the lowest number of fires recorded in the Amazon in 41 years - is positive news, but it does not yet allow us to conclude that this is an established trend or to scale back prevention efforts," Arruda added.
The MapBiomas report shows a dramatic drop in area burned not just in the Amazon, but across the whole of Brazil in 2025.
Figures show around 12.7 million hectares burned in Brazil in 2025, compared to 30 million hectares in 2024.
The highest number of hectares burned in Brazil since records began was in 2007, when 30.7 million were recorded across the country.
The decline in the 2025 figures partly reflects an easing of the unprecedented fires of 2024, helped by cooler La Niña conditions instead of the warmer El Niño.
But MapBiomas warned the natural weather pattern of El Niño, which pushes up global temperatures, could extend this year's dry season and increase the risk of forest fires.
Tropical rainforests like the Amazon are home to millions of species, and in a healthy state they absorb vast quantities of planet-warming carbon dioxide, helping to keep the Earth cool.
They have come under increasing pressure as a result of decades of deliberate land clearance for agriculture and logging, as well as climate change, which scientists warn can create the conditions for bigger fires to spread.
When he took office, President Lula promised to reverse the deforestation which occurred during the presidency of his predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro argued that more farming and mining in the Amazon would reduce poverty in the region and environmentalists accused him of allowing deforestation to accelerate.
Three years into Bolsonaro's four-year term, the amount of trees cut down in the Amazon rainforest went up by 75%.
On his first day in office, on 1 January 2023, Lula insisted that "our goal is to achieve zero deforestation in the Amazon".
While that pledge was warmly welcomed by environmentalists, there has been widespread criticism of Lula's decision to approve oil exploration at the mouth of the Amazon river, which activists say flies in the face of his promise to protect the Amazon region.

title: Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10 million
summary: The water company said the three heatwaves contributed to the ban.
full_text:
Thames Water announces hosepipe ban for 10 million
- Published
Thames Water has announced a hosepipe ban affecting 10.1 million customers after an "exceptionally warm and dry spring".
The restrictions mean, from Thursday, hosepipes should not be used for watering gardens or allotments, cleaning cars, filling paddling pools or swimming pools, or cleaning windows.
The water company said its region had seen 40% of average rainfall, and more days at or above 34C this year than ever recorded before.
Nevil Muncaster, director of strategic water resources, said: "We would not be taking this step unless it was necessary to protect water supplies for everyone and the environment."
The ban applies to all customers that Thames Water supplies with drinking water and comes into effect on Thursday.
The company provides water to customers across parts of Gloucestershire, Wiltshire, Surrey, the Thames Valley, Greater London, and the surrounding areas, external.
It provides water and wastewater services to 16 million customers overall.
It said water use was currently 10% above normal in the Thames Valley and Home Counties and 7% above normal in London, which amounted to an extra 100 million litres of water every day.
Muncaster added: "Recent heatwaves and a very dry spring and summer have led to sustained high demand.
"While there is enough water for essential use, we need to reduce non-essential outdoor demand to keep taps flowing."
He said teams were "working 24/7 to keep water moving, fix leaks and support customers" and that the situation would be kept "under close review", with restrictions lifted when safe to do so.
The company said this year's hot weather had meant during peak periods "water has been used faster than it can be treated and moved through parts of the network, placing additional pressure on local supplies".
"Customers should continue to use water for essential needs such as drinking, cooking, washing and hygiene," it said.
"Buckets and watering cans can still be used, and there are exemptions, including where water use is necessary for health and safety reasons or for customers with severe mobility problems."
Thames Water is about £20bn in debt.
The government recently rejected a rescue proposal, and the BBC understands the company's main lenders are preparing a legal challenge in case the new Andy Burnham-led government takes the firm into public hands.
Do's and don'ts
Hosepipes and pressure washers should not be used to:
- water gardens, lawns, or allotments (this includes the use of sprinklers) 
- fill paddling pools, swimming pools, or hot tubs 
- clean vehicles, patios, paths, driveways, walls, windows, or any outdoor areas 
Plants and gardens can be watered with a watering can, and cars can be washed using a bucket
Some exemptions may include:
- Wastewater only customers 
- Health and safety needs 
- Animal welfare, including pets, livestock, and fish 
- Watering food crops and certain newly planted trees 
- Customers who cannot reasonably adjust their water use because of a disability or medical condition 
Source: Thames Water, external
Bans in force
Elsewhere, South East Water has announced that a hosepipe ban currently in force in Kent will be extended to parts of Surrey, Sussex, Hampshire and Berkshire from Saturday.
Other companies with bans in force include Southern Water, which affects about one million customers across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, and South West Water, covering Mid Devon and other parts of the county, and Lyme Regis in Dorset.
A ban affecting 33,000 properties in west Wales was introduced last weekend by Welsh Water.
Cambridge Water, Anglian Water and Affinity Water, which all supply to much of the East of England, have implemented "temporary use bans".
The UK's summer has seen a number of records broken - including some which date back to the notorious summer of 1976 in which a drought was declared and a minister appointed to deal with water problems.
A lack of rain has also been a big part of this summer with some places in southern England seeing no measurable rain for more than four weeks.
Correction: The earlier figure in this story has been amended to 10 million because only Thames Water's water supply customers, and not waste water customers, are affected.

title: Ryanair boss says 'foreign object' may have caused plane window incident
summary: Passenger Ljubisa Karović was partially sucked out of a cabin window on the Boeing aircraft.
full_text:
Ryanair broken window may have been caused by 'foreign object'
- Published
An incident on a Ryanair flight which saw a passenger partially sucked out of a plane window may have been caused by "foreign object damage" to an engine, said the airline's boss.
Michael O'Leary said an initial investigation into the incident on 10 July between Greece and Germany suggests "it looks like a foreign object damage to the engine on takeoff at Thessaloniki but ... we can't say that definitively".
He insisted that the engine on the 18-year-old Boeing 737 plane had been fully serviced and overhauled in the past two years.
Serbian national Ljubisa Karović's head and right shoulder were sucked out of the plane's window, leaving him "seriously injured and in shock".
His wife Svetlana Grković Maksimović told BBC Serbia that she and two other passengers held on to his legs for several minutes.
She said: "We pulled him back together. His entire face was deformed and blood was pouring from his nose and mouth."
He was taken to hospital after the plane made an emergency landing.
Passengers told local media they heard "some kind of explosion" on board.
The aircraft was operated by Ryanair's subsidiary Malta Air.
Confirmation that the damage was caused by an external object could affect Ryanair or Boeing's liabilities over the incident.
The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. O'Leary said that a draft report would be issued in about 28 days.

title: Lindt's Easter chocolate sales fall after price hike
summary: The Swiss chocolate maker adjusts its strategy in response to weaker demand after its price rises.
full_text:
Lindt's Easter chocolate sales fall after price hike
- Published
Lindt has partially U-turned on its decision to hike prices after Easter chocolate sales dropped.
The Swiss chocolate maker said a "necessary groupwide" price surge of 11.8% was one of the reasons revenue shrank in the first half of this year, particularly in the UK, Germany, and Switzerland.
It also blamed weaker Easter demand and a drop in tourism from Asia and the Middle East "due to geopolitical uncertainties". In response, it said it has adjusted prices and boosted marketing in certain regions for the second half of the year.
Around Easter, Lindt is known for its chocolate rabbits wrapped in gold-coloured foil and decorated with a red ribbon and bell on their necks.
Overall, the company's sales dipped 0.9%, with European sales down by 2.1%. It added that "performance was impacted by more price-sensitive and mature markets such as Germany, Switzerland and the UK".
By volume, meaning the amount of chocolate sold rather than the money it made, overall sales sank 7.5%. Pre-tax profit fell 1.5%.
Meanwhile, sales of Lindt chocolate in airports decreased "due to ongoing conflicts in the Middle East, and therefore declining passenger traffic".
Lindt said it sales picked up in North America, Australia, China, and Japan, though these countries account for a much smaller slice of its sales than Europe, where it makes over half its revenue.
Lindt chief executive Adalbert Lechner said: "The actions we have initiated focus on volume recovery in the second half of 2026 and lay the foundation to regain volume growth momentum in 2027."
Lindt is not the only chocolate firm which has been putting prices up.
Experts say climate change has led to extreme rainfall and droughts which have decreased cocoa farmers' crops.
This pushes up costs of making chocolate, and companies have chosen different ways to react to this, with some reducing chocolate content or sizes rather than raising prices.
According to the latest official data, the annual rate of chocolate and sweet price rises is 7.9%, external – much higher than the general rate of UK inflation at 2.8%, external.

title: VAT to be cut from household electricity bills in October
summary: Homes will save around £45 a year through the cut announced on Andy Burnham's first full day as prime minister.
full_text:
VAT to be cut from household electricity bills in October
- Published
VAT will be cut from household electricity bills, the government has announced, as part of new Prime Minister Andy Burnham's pledge to help with the cost of living.
The reduction from 5% VAT to zero will come into effect on 1 October, saving a typical household about £45 a year.
Ministers said it would be funded by savings from the cancellation of the digital ID programme, which was going to cost £1.8bn over the next three years. The government estimated it will cost £850m this financial year.
But Labour's Darren Jones, who was sacked as chief secretary to the prime minister on Monday, accused the government of announcing an unfunded tax cut.
- What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? - Published7 hours ago
 
- Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high - Published1 hour ago
 
Jonathan Reynolds, the new business secretary, said the cut would give people some "breathing space".
He said it was funded until "the end of the financial year" in March 2027 and any changes beyond that would have to be announced in the next Budget.
Suppliers have been told the VAT reduction should be passed on to all household customers, including those on fixed tariffs, as was the case when some charges were taken off bills in April.
The cut will take effect in England, Scotland and Wales, but equivalent funding would be given to Northern Ireland, which is regulated differently, the government said.
The reduction could not be automatically be applied in Northern Ireland due to EU rules limiting the range of goods which can be sold without VAT. Following Brexit, England, Scotland and Wales are not bound by these restrictions.
Small businesses who qualify for the domestic energy VAT relief and are not registered for VAT, as well as charities and residential care homes eligible for the reduced rate, will also benefit.
Cutting VAT is a relatively basic tool to reduce an energy bill - with larger households likely to save more as they use more electricity.
However, some vulnerable households are also high electricity users, such as for running medical equipment.
Jones, who was also previously chief secretary to the Treasury, wrote on X, external that the Digital ID programme was unfunded.
While praising the VAT cut as "good", he said "the government will have to set out how it will pay for its new policies at the budget".
Conservative Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride also criticised the use of the Digital ID budget to fund the VAT cut.
"The cuts to the Digital ID card budget are not real because the money was never provided in the first place.
"We are only one day in and already it is smoke and mirrors on the public finances."
Reynolds told the BBC's Today programme a VAT cut to electricity bills would be funded through a "straightforward switch spend" redirecting money for digital ID.
He said money for digital ID "would have had to have been found" and that scrapping the scheme removed "pressure" from the budget allowing the government to "give real help to people".
But the Office for Budget Responsibility said last November that digital ID would have to paid for out of savings from government departments and these had not yet been identified.
The spending watchdog said bringing in Digital ID had "provisionally forecast to cost £1.8bn in total over the next three years".
Government sources have insisted that departments have been working to find savings to fund Digital ID since the OBR made its forecast in November and this money would now be reallocated to fund the VAT cut.
Household energy prices rose by 13% for millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales at the start of July, under regulator Ofgem's price cap.
Price rises were driven by the higher cost of gas, but have a relatively limited impact owing to warm weather and lower energy use during the summer months.
However, higher energy prices caused by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has constrained global supplies of oil and liquified natural gas, are likely to persist into the winter, according to analysts.
The VAT cut only applies to the current financial year — any decision to keep it in future years would have to be made in a Budget.
The government expects it will lower inflation by 0.1 percentage points.
In his first speech as the UK's prime minister, Burnham vowed to provide "breathing space" for households struggling with the cost of living.
On Tuesday, he said the VAT cut would "put more money in people's pockets".
The VAT cut is the second intervention on energy bills by the government in six months.
Former chancellor Rachel Reeves removed one levy and shifted others onto general taxation to lower bills in April.
Speaking to the BBC, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said: "I think we'll have a summer of these little headline grabbing small announcements.
"What we need is the big picture so people know they are getting real help with the cost of living."
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the VAT cut was "something that is only allowed because of Brexit".
But he said it would not "address the real issue of the cost of living" and of running a home, because "most houses are heated by oil or gas" and bills were being inflated by green levies.
The End Fuel Poverty Coalition welcomed the reduction, but said it "does not address the scale of what households are facing".
Simon Francis, the group's co-ordinator, said Burnham's government must "go even further" with targeted support for those most in need.
He added: "This breathing space is also not a cure. The only way to bring bills down for good is to change how they are set."

title: Angela Rayner: Cabinet comeback for one of Labour's biggest names
summary: The potential contender to replace Keir Starmer is now back in the cabinet under Andy Burnham.
full_text:
Angela Rayner: Cabinet comeback for one of Labour's biggest names
- Published
Earlier this year, Angela Rayner was weighing up whether to reach for the Labour crown if Sir Keir Starmer's leadership was challenged.
The resolution of an HMRC investigation into her tax affairs, long seen as a barrier to any leadership bid, cleared a path for the former deputy prime minister to take part in any contest to replace her old boss.
But in the end she added her name to the wave of Labour MPs nominating Andy Burnham as leader, propelling the former Greater Manchester mayor into Downing Street uncontested.
Now she has made a return to the cabinet, with Burnham giving her back the job of housing secretary from which she resigned in September last year, after admitting she did not pay enough tax on the purchase of a new home.
It is a role in which she will play a key part in his drive to devolve power away from Westminster and deliver a major programme of council house building.
Her against-the-odds story, personality, and ability to connect with parts of the electorate other politicians have struggled to reach are likely to make her a prominent voice within Burnham's top team.
Tough upbringing
Born Angela Bowen in Stockport, Greater Manchester, in 1980, Rayner grew up on one of the area's poorest council estates and from an early age was caring for her mother, who had bipolar disorder and suffered from depression.
Both Rayner's parents were unemployed and speaking in 2017, she remembered having to grow up very quickly.
"My mum was a really vulnerable person. I remember, at 10, my mum being suicidal and me sleeping like a dog on the end of her bed, just to try and stay next to her so she didn't do any harm to herself," Rayner said.
She has also recalled going to her grandmother's flat on Sundays, so the family could take it in turns to have a bath there. Hot water was too expensive for them to use at home.
- Angela Rayner's explosive speech reignites leadership speculation - Published18 March
 
- Angela Rayner settles tax bill with HMRC - Published14 May
 
- Angela Rayner resigns after underpaying tax on Hove flat - Published5 September 2025
 
Rayner has often spoken about being told she would "never amount to anything", after she left school without any qualifications.
But after having her first child at 16, Rayner studied part-time at college, learning British sign language and gaining a vocational qualification in social care.
She spent a number of years as a care worker in Stockport, mainly looking after elderly people in their own homes, while also rising quickly through the ranks of the union, Unison.
She has described herself as "mouthy", someone who would "take no messing from management".
In her 20s, she became a full-time union official and eventually, after battles over working conditions and zero-hour contracts, rose to the most senior elected role in Unison in north-west England.
It was at Unison she met Mark Rayner, a fellow union official whom she married in 2010 and divorced in 2023. The couple went on to have two sons, one of whom was born so prematurely he is registered blind and has special educational needs.
At the age of 37, the mum-of-three became a grandmother, sparking the nickname "Grangela".
She credits the trade union movement with encouraging her to enter politics and taking her from - in her own words - "the girl on a council estate" to "a woman who feels like she can conquer the world".
Those ambitions started to be realised in 2015, when she was elected as the MP for Ashton-under-Lyne - a seat not far from her hometown. She later said she had only stood to make the point that "people like me can't get elected" and had "accidentally" won the seat.
The Prescott role
A self-described "proper working-class" woman, Rayner rose quickly in Westminster, taking up the women and equalities and education briefs in the shadow cabinet of former Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.
When Corbyn stood down in 2020, following Labour's worst general election result since 1935, Rayner did not run for the leadership, and backed her ally Rebecca Long-Bailey, who came second to Sir Keir.
Instead, Rayner stood for the deputy leadership and won election to that post comfortably - going on to be a central figure in Sir Keir's bid to remake the party.
However, relations between Sir Keir and Rayner were sometimes tense. After Labour lost control of eight English councils and lost the seat of Hartlepool in a parliamentary by-election in May 2021, the deputy leader was removed from her post as party chairwoman.
She pushed back, and was appointed shadow first secretary of state among other titles.
By that point, Rayner had a strong support base and a powerful role likened to that of John Prescott, who was seen as a political bridge between the working class and the New Labour project during Tony Blair's premiership.
Rayner heavily leaned into that role and tried to use it to her party's advantage in the years before Labour's general election win in 2024.
Outspoken and combative at times, Rayner repeatedly accused the Conservatives of being "out of touch", and hammered the party with lines such as "one rule for them and another rule for us" during the scandal over pandemic parties in Downing Street.
Sometimes Rayner admitted she had gone too far, once apologising for describing senior Conservatives as "a bunch of scum".
Her prominence and the venom of her political attacks had put a target on her back and attracted unwanted headlines.
In 2021, Rayner lashed out at "sexism and misogyny" in politics, after a newspaper reported that she crossed and uncrossed her legs during prime minister's questions to distract Boris Johnson.
And in 2024, she was investigated by the police over the tax paid on the sale of her council house, again following a slew of reports by unfriendly newspapers, cheered on by the Conservatives. She was not found to have committed a criminal offence.
Her tendency to brush through political controversies gave her an air of untouchability, with some dubbing her "Teflon Ange".
Her stock had risen further still as deputy prime minister, leading on one of Labour's key pledges to build 1.5 million homes by 2030, and helping Sir Keir quell a rebellion by Labour MPs over welfare cuts.
But the political optics of a housing secretary admitting she had not paid enough when buying her £800,000 flat in Hove were not easy on the eye.
Rayner faced charges of hypocrisy and calls for her to stand down, and she did so after admitting arrangements on her family home in Greater Manchester meant she should have paid a higher rate.
She resigned from government after the prime minister's ethics adviser Sir Laurie Magnus declared that she had breached the ministerial code.
HMRC launched an investigation, and almost 10 months later, as a leadership crisis engulfed her party, a conclusion was reached.
Rayner announced she had settled £40,000 in unpaid stamp duty, and had been "exonerated" of the accusation she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".
In an interview with the Guardian, the prime minister's former deputy did not rule out running in any Labour leadership race but said she would not "trigger" a contest.
Pressed over whether the prime minister should step aside, Rayner said: "Keir will have to reflect on that."
Prior to his downfall as Labour leader, Sir Keir had suggested he could bring Rayner back into his cabinet, adding she had the "best social mobility story this country has ever seen".
It is a story she will be hoping to continue after her return to cabinet, as Labour heads in a new direction under Burnham.

title: Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high
summary: The government has announced it will cut VAT on domestic electricity to zero but Britons still pay more for power than many other European nations.
full_text:
Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high
- Published
While the UK government has announced it will cut VAT on domestic electricity this October from 5% to zero in an attempt to help with the cost of living, British households are still paying more for power than many other European nations.
Comparing UK prices with the EU shows that medium-use households here paid the fourth-highest electricity prices in the second half of last year including taxes and levies, although the government has taken steps to reduce bills since then.
Here are three key reasons why British electricity prices are high.
1. The cost of wholesale gas often sets the electricity price
The price energy suppliers pay for electricity is set by a bidding process with each generating company saying what it would be willing to accept to produce one unit of electricity.
Once built, the cost of generating power from renewables like wind and solar is relatively low, so these typically come in with the cheapest bid. Nuclear might come next.
Gas generators often have the highest costs because they have to buy fuel to generate electricity as well as paying a "carbon price" - a charge for emissions.
The wholesale cost is set by the last unit of electricity needed to meet demand from consumers.
This means that even if gas only generates 1% of overall electricity at a given time it can often set the overall wholesale price which gets paid to every type of generator.
That raises prices for households - particularly because the wars in Iran and Ukraine have increased the cost of gas.
Northern Ireland operates on a separate system to the rest of the UK, being part of the Single Electricity Market with the Republic of Ireland.
2. Other countries have a different energy mix
Analysts say that one of the reasons why electricity prices are higher in the UK than some other countries is because we generate a relatively high share of our electricity from natural gas.
In 2025 31% of the UK's electricity was produced from burning natural gas.
This compares with just 3% in France, which generated the majority of its electricity - 69% - from nuclear power.
The US has a higher share of natural gas in its electricity generation mix than the UK - 40% - but American wholesale gas prices are considerably lower thanks to the shale gas production boom of the past 20 years.
3. The UK is building much more electricity grid infrastructure
Higher wholesale gas prices have pushed up UK domestic electricity bills this year.
The wholesale energy costs contribution to a typical household bill in Great Britain rose from £311 in 2024-25 to £320 in 2025-26.
But bills have also been pushed up in recent years by state subsidies to encourage private firms to build wind and solar farms and also national electricity grid network investment costs, which previous governments have added to household electricity bills.
These network costs have been driven by the need to expand and modernise the grid to accommodate new wind and solar farms and transmit their power to homes and businesses.
The network costs contribution to a typical bill rose from £136 in 2019-20 to £250 in 2026, an increase of £113.
"We've probably underinvested in the last decade and now we're trying to catch up so there's quite a lot of spending," says Frankie Mayo, an energy analyst from Ember Energy.
The generation subsidies contribution to a typical bill rose from £127 in 2019-20 to £159 in 2026, an increase of £32.
Network costs are projected to increase further by 2030, adding another £48 to a typical bill, according to calculations by energy analyst Ben James.
However the government and some energy groups also argue that reducing our national reliance on volatile international gas prices via the government's 2030 clean power policy will keep down the UK's wholesale electricity costs and mean household bills will be lower than they would otherwise have been.
This would be by reducing the amount of time in each year that gas sets the wholesale electricity price.
A great deal though depends on future wholesale gas prices which are impossible to accurately forecast.
Some analysts, including the government's Climate Change Committee, also say the government should go further to remove policy costs from household electricity bills and meet them through general taxation instead, in order to avoid discouraging people from using electricity rather than gas to heat their homes.
"The way you allocate those costs matters," says Mayo.
"They may be being put on bills or they may be being paid by consumers in other ways that are less visible, such as taxes."

title: Why Iran is risking so much over the Strait of Hormuz
summary: None of the choices facing Iran’s leaders offer a clear path to victory, as the conflict with the US continues.
full_text:
Why Iran is risking so much over the Strait of Hormuz
- Published
After 10 days of exchanging strikes with the US over control of the vital Strait of Hormuz waterway, Iran's leaders may appear to have three choices. None offer a clear route to victory.
The first is to accept much of what Washington wants: guarantee free and safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz by ending attacks on commercial shipping, give up or dilute Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium, and accept intrusive inspections by the global nuclear watchdog.
In return, Tehran would seek an end to the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, and protection from further attacks.
This is probably the least costly option, but also the costliest politically.
Reopening Hormuz without securing a recognised Iranian role in managing the waterway would mean surrendering what some in Tehran increasingly see as a newly discovered deterrent, one that may now appear more effective than Iran's missiles, regional proxies, or even its nuclear programme.
For the first time, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated its ability to impose immediate costs on the global economy for an attack on its territory by its enemies.
The nuclear programme, meanwhile, has long been presented as a right that Iran cannot be forced to abandon.
Conceding to demands for tight restrictions on nuclear activities after months of attacks would allow hardliners to argue that American military pressure had worked. It could also open the door to further demands over Iran's missile programme and its relationships with Hezbollah in Lebanon, Iraqi Shia groups and Yemen's Houthis.
The second option is escalation. Iran could intensify its attacks on American bases in the region, shipping, and vital infrastructure in Gulf Arab states, hoping that higher energy prices and wider disruption would force Washington and its allies to compromise.
This carries the greatest military risk. An attack causing mass casualties or serious damage to Gulf infrastructure could draw Iran's neighbours more directly into the conflict and leave it facing a broader coalition.
The third option is to preserve the current instability: enough pressure on shipping and energy markets to retain leverage, but not enough to trigger a return to all-out war with the US.
This seems to fit the Islamic Republic's established thinking. Iran does not need to defeat a stronger enemy if it can survive for longer than that enemy is willing to fight. Survival itself can be presented as victory. But sanctions, war damage and inflation are steadily increasing pressure at home.
And as time goes on, a paradox may emerge: The more Iran uses the Strait of Hormuz as a weapon, the less powerful it could become if countries find new ways to export energy and other goods out of the region.
Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has acknowledged the contradiction, arguing that the value of Hormuz lies in increasing the volume of shipping through it rather than reducing it. A permanently unsafe waterway encourages the world to find ways around Iran.
- Why the Strait of Hormuz matters so much in the Iran war - Published7 days ago
 
Who is making the decisions
Complicating matters further is the uncertainty surrounding Iran's decision-making process.
Under Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in a strike at the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran in February, disputes between elected politicians, clerical institutions and the Revolutionary Guards were ultimately settled by the supreme leader. After months of war and under the new leadership of Khamenei's son Mojtaba, that balance of power is less clear.
President Masoud Pezeshkian and his diplomats may favour a settlement to ease economic pressure and restore stability. Hardliners in parliament, powerful unelected institutions, and conservative media outlets, meanwhile, may fear that major concessions would undermine the ideological foundations of the Islamic Republic and alienate its core supporters.
The biggest question concerns the armed forces, particularly the Revolutionary Guards. Iran's missile programme, regional alliances and strategy in the Strait of Hormuz are central to the Revolutionary Guards' influence, yet it remains unclear how much weight commanders carry in decisions over escalation and negotiations.
The three options facing Tehran do not impose the same costs on different parts of the system. Pragmatists may favour a deal, hardliners may prefer endurance, while some military commanders could see escalation as strengthening Iran's bargaining position.
The question, therefore, is not only which path Iran chooses, but who has the authority to make that choice.
What Iranians are saying
The leadership's idea of endurance looks very different to those required to endure it.
Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June to halt military operations and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days. But three weeks after it was signed, US President Donald Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in Hormuz, and US strikes in response.
One woman in Iran told BBC Persian that she was "very, very saddened" when the fighting resumed.
She had hoped the MoU would give the two sides time to resolve the remaining disputes and restore stability. Instead, she fears the destruction of infrastructure and the deaths of civilians and military personnel.
She blamed hardliners inside the Iranian system for imposing destructive policies, while also condemning opposition figures abroad who, in her view, had encouraged war.
Another woman in Tehran said the foreign-trade company where she worked had closed, leaving her unemployed for four months despite holding a doctorate and having 17 years of experience.
"No-one is hiring because nobody knows what will happen," she said. She described soaring prices, power and water cuts, increased theft, and occasional gunfire at night. She now limits how often she travels around the city.
These accounts do not point to a single political conclusion. Foreign attacks can produce anger against the United States and Israel even among opponents of the Islamic Republic. But they also illustrate the limits of asking the public to endure indefinite hardship in the name of resistance.
Trump faces difficult choices of his own: widen the war, continue military and economic pressure, or accept a settlement allowing Iran a restricted civilian nuclear programme under stronger supervision. None offers a clear path to victory.
The confrontation could continue for months through cycles of attacks, mediation and temporary ceasefires. The decisive question is how long Iran's leaders can preserve Hormuz as leverage without provoking an all-out war, renewed unrest or the construction of alternative routes that make the strait matter less.
