'Without us, there's no way they can survive': Trump defends new tariffs on Canada
In the Oval Office today, Donald Trump defended the new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods.
“Canada has been very, very tough on us over the years, for many years, and no other president’s done anything about it,” Trump said. “In all fairness to them, they need us to survive. Without us, there’s no way they can survive.”
This week, the White House said that the new levies were because Canada has unfairly discriminated against American cars, alcohol and dairy products. The tariffs will go into effect in 30 days, leaving time for possible discussions between the two countries.
Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister, said that he spoke with Trump earlier on Tuesday. “We agreed to intensify negotiations in the coming weeks, and the team and myself look forward to doing that,” Carney told reporters.
The tariffs will hit a wide range of products, the White House said, including wine, hockey sticks and cement. They also include goods previously protected from import taxes under the United States-Mexico-Canada (USMCA) agreement.
Trump told members of the press that the latest round of tariffs was not in response to the Canadian wildfire smoke that spread across North America last week, and the president railed against.
On Friday, Trump blasted Canada for its response to the persistent wildfires and the smoke that affected about 109 million people across the midwest, mid-Atlantic and north-east. “The cost is incalculable!” Trump raged on social media. “This is Willful Negligence, and becoming a yearly occurrence, costing the United States Billions of Dollars, which cost of this pollution must of necessity be added to the TARIFFS Canada is currently paying.”
However, the president told reporters on Tuesday that his administration is looking at those tariffs “separately”.
Trump administration halts more than $1bn in Medicaid funding to California and Minnesota
Melody Schreiber
The Trump administration has paused more than $1bn in Medicaid funding to California and Minnesota, citing “suspected fraud and noncompliance” – withholding of funding that follows a $243m pause in Medicaid payments to Minnesota earlier this year.
“If those states want that money, they need to provide documentation that these payments are legitimate,” said Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), said at a press conference on Tuesday.
Officials relied on AI to identify potential fraud, Kennedy said. “We used AI, advanced analytics, and other cutting-edge tools to identify suspicious activity and potential fraud.”
The pause includes more than $867m for California and about $200m for Minnesota.
In California, most of the suspected fraud was in in-home services, he said. Kennedy has several times singled out in-home care provision, which can be a lifeline for disabled individuals – rhetoric that has worried families and angered lawmakers.
Vice-President JD Vance threatened in March to withhold funding to states if they did not cooperate with a new fraud taskforce, headed by Vance and established by a White House executive order.
A US appeals court has overturned a ruling that ordered the Donald Trump administration to release pro-Palestinian activist Mohsen Mahdawi from immigration detention.
The decision came from the 2nd US circuit court of appeals which found that the lower court did not have jurisdiction to hear the case concerning the 35-year old Palestinian green card holder.
“We conclude that the district court should not have reached this question,” US Circuit Judge Debra Ann Livingston wrote.
In response to the ruling, Michael Tan, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, who argued on behalf of Mr. Mahdawi last year, said: “The government is claiming the unprecedented power to detain people for months or even years on end to censor their speech, with no ability to challenge their detention in court. This is as absurd as it is dangerous.”
We will continue to fight for our client and for his right to prompt judicial review,” Tan added.
Tuesday’s ruling follows a a decision earlier this year by an immigration judge who blocked the Trump administration from deporting Mahdawi, who secretary of state Marco Rubio has claimed “would have potentially serious adverse foreign policy consequences for the United States.”
Mahdawi, a Columbia University student, was detained by federal agents in Vermont last year during his citizenship interview.
A software error in New Jersey’s motor vehicle system mistakenly registered about 6,600 people who identified themselves as non-US citizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024, New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill said on Tuesday.
Sherrill said that individuals “answered ‘no’ when asked on a keypad whether they were a US citizen when applying for drivers’ licenses and identification cards, but through no fault of their own, the system registered them anyway.”
She added that the error occured under the previous administration and that she has since ordered the removal of any residents from voter rolls that were mistakenly added during that time period.
“Our preliminary analysis shows fewer than 400 individuals who were newly registered for the first time because of the error voted. They were registered as Democrats, Republicans and Unaffiliated voters and were scattered across the state,” Sherrill said.
She went on to say that she is “appalled by the reckless failures that allowed this to happen and the lack of transparency shown by those in charge at the time.”
“This failure didn’t occur under my watch, but accountability starts now. I am taking action to prevent anything like it from occurring in the future and make sure those responsible are held accountable,” she continued.

It warns that changes in US policy risk reversing progress in the fight against HIV/Aids.

title: Spanish hotel chain ceases operations in Cuba under pressure from Washington
summary:
Meliá group says Donald Trump’s sanctions make it ‘impossible’ to keep any of its 34 sites open

A Spanish hotel chain is to cease all operations in Cuba at the end of the week due to “major difficulties” in doing business on the island under growing pressure from Washington.

The latest US sanctions make it “impossible, de facto and de jure, to maintain even minimal operational stability”, the Meliá group explained in a statement on Tuesday to the Spanish stock market regulator.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A Spanish hotel chain is to cease all operations in Cuba at the end of the week due to “major difficulties” in doing business on the island under growing pressure from Washington.
The latest US sanctions make it “impossible, de facto and de jure, to maintain even minimal operational stability”, the Meliá group explained in a statement on Tuesday to the Spanish stock market regulator.
The company said it would strive to ensure a smooth transition to reduce the impact as much as possible on staff, suppliers and clients.
Meliá announced last month that it would cease operating 15 of its 34 hotels in Cuba, joining other foreign companies that have cut ties with the island’s military conglomerate, GAESA, under pressure from Washington.
Meliá, one of the largest foreign hotel operators in Cuba with 14,000 rooms, did not refer in that statement to the other 19 hotels it operated in Cuba in partnership with the country’s tourism ministry.
Donald Trump, the US president, ordered new sanctions in May against Cuba, targeting a broad set of individuals and threatening foreign banks and companies that worked with them.
Meliá was the first Spanish hotel group to establish a presence in Cuba after the Caribbean nation opened its tourism sector to foreigners in the 1990s, hoping to ease the economic crisis triggered by the collapse of the Soviet Union.
In addition to an economic embargo in place since 1962, Washington has blocked all oil shipments to the island since January, with the exception of a single Russian ship.

title: US claims of Cuba’s ‘unique threat’ jar with reality of hunger and blackouts
summary:
State department’s 100-page report is latest push in Trump administration campaign to bring down government

The US government’s latest allegations that Cuba is behind “many of the most significant upheavals in recent American political history” and that its leaders pose “a unique threat to American homeland security” have come as startling revelations to those living under the six-month-long US oil blockade in Havana, where desperate people search through piles of uncollected rubbish for food, or else swelter at home in 24-hour-plus blackouts.

The unsigned 100-page report, Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism, published by the US state department on Monday, blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”.

full_text:
The US government’s latest allegations that Cuba is behind “many of the most significant upheavals in recent American political history” and that its leaders pose “a unique threat to American homeland security” have come as startling revelations to those living under the six-month-long US oil blockade in Havana, where desperate people search through piles of uncollected rubbish for food, or else swelter at home in 24-hour-plus blackouts.
The unsigned 100-page report, Cuba: Capital of 21st-Century Communism, published by the US state department on Monday, blames Havana for everything from “the George Floyd riots to the rise of antifa to the explosion of pro-terrorist activism on American college campuses”.
It is the latest push in a maximum-pressure campaign to bring down the island’s government that began with the abduction of Nicolás Maduro, the president of Cuba’s ally Venezuela, on 3 January. Since then, Cuba has been brought to a standstill by the oil blockade, sanctions on foreign businesses and threats of a military intervention.
It also seems to be an attempt to “other” those on the US left before November’s midterm elections.
“Cuba’s assault on the United States was never, at root, a quarrel over economic policy or sovereignty or even ownership of a particular territory,” the report reads. “It was a revolution against western civilisation itself – waged, in part, via the novel and insidious method of persuading the children of the west to turn against their own inheritance.”
“Fidel would have been quite proud of this,” said one amused Cuban as he read it.
The US state department, run by the Cuban-American Marco Rubio, refused to name the author, but it is clearly someone who knows their history. “Almost immediately after taking Havana in January 1959, Castro began plotting armed assaults against neighbouring governments – launching expeditions against Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Nicaragua and Panama in just that year alone,” it reads.
What it fails to mention is that Haiti was then run by François “Papa Doc” Duvalier, who killed an estimated 60,000 of his own people; the Dominican Republic by Rafael Trujillo, who launched the “parsley massacre”, killing between 20,000 to 35,000 Haitians; and Nicaragua by the Somoza family, who are credited with the murder of up to 50,000 Nicaraguans.
Although the report provides no new evidence, there is a suspicious emphasis on race. The supposedly remarkable success of Cuban intelligence at infiltrating US institutions was due to a soft spot for “glamorous Latins”, it quotes an intelligence officer saying to the Miami Herald in 2002: “‘We’re much more open to Latins than we are to people with steel teeth and a Slavic accent.’”
It also bemoans the ideological commitment of the spies Cuba recruited, while failing to mention either that several were inspired by the CIA’s attempts to assassinate Castro, or the shelter the US offered to the exiles Luis Posada Carriles and Orlando Bosch, who organised the bombing of Cubana flight 455 in 1976, killing 73 people.
Most jarringly, the report groups together the US’s long internal struggle around civil rights and social reform and reframes it as a battle between the forces of foreign actors and “western civilisation”, lingering over groups such as the Black Panthers, which it credits to Cuba.
While several black revolutionaries found sanctuary on the island, most famously Assata Shakur, who had a $2m price on her head for the killing of a New Jersey state trooper, the experience was not perhaps as conspiratorial as the author suggests. In interviews, Nehanda Abiodun, one of the mentioned fugitives, said her politics and revolutionary rage came from her experience growing up in 1970s New York, not out of any love for Cuba, whose government she came to resent for muzzling her in return for refuge. She used to say that the first thing that happened on landing was being racially profiled by the Cuban police. If she was part of a well-oiled international conspiracy, it didn’t show.
For five years the Cuban government has not even been able to afford to feed its 9.5 million people, who mostly blame it for the crisis. But the report is ready for this: “To mistake Cuba’s poverty for harmlessness is to misunderstand the threat entirely. Its material weakness was never the measure of its danger.”
It concludes: “Today, Cuban agents and operatives maintain a foothold in hundreds of front groups, activist organisations, solidarity centres, and ideological NGO and nonprofit networks. These groups collectively represent one of the single largest, most sophisticated and dangerous vectors for hostile foreign influence in modern American history.”
In the run-up to the report’s release, Miguel Díaz-Canel, Cuba’s president, said the US had fallen prey to a “new and more dangerous version of McCarthyism”.
But perhaps the more damning criticism came from a Cuban academic who preferred to remain nameless: “It reads just like a report Cuba’s state media might write about the United States.”

title: We received no alert, say leaders of First Nations communities razed by Canadian wildfires
summary:
Chiefs in Ontario say they were left to self-evacuate before homes burned to ground, after being told there was no imminent threat

Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts.

Thirteen communities in Ontario province have been ordered to evacuate because of wildfires, most of them First Nations. The Ontario premier, Doug Ford, told reporters on Monday that close to 2,000 people had been evacuated so far to cities including Toronto and Niagara Falls.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Fast-moving wildfires have burned two First Nations communities in Canada to the ground, as members said they were left to self-evacuate without government help or emergency alerts.
Thirteen communities in Ontario province have been ordered to evacuate because of wildfires, most of them First Nations. The Ontario premier, Doug Ford, told reporters on Monday that close to 2,000 people had been evacuated so far to cities including Toronto and Niagara Falls.
There are nearly 1,000 wildfires burning across Canada, with about 200 in Ontario. The prime minister, Mark Carney, said heatwaves and dry weather had combined to create “one of the most intense wildfire seasons in Canadian history”.
Namaygoosisagagun First Nation, located north of Thunder Bay in north-western Ontario, was engulfed by fire on 15 June. About two dozen people quickly boarded boats packed with their possessions and raced across the nearby lake.
“If this community waited for a mandatory evacuation process, we’d be doing a recovery mission for the bodies of children, of elders, of men and women,” said Linda Debassige, grand council chief of the Anishinabek Nation, which represents 39 Ontario First Nations.
All members safely escaped but the community’s buildings and other infrastructure were completely destroyed. The Namaygoosisagagun people evacuated to Thunder Bay, where the Anishinabek Nation has been providing assistance.
Debassige said that Namaygoosisagagun’s chief, Helen Paavola, had made inquiries to the federal government in the days leading up to the fire, but the community had been assured there was no imminent threat.
Ford travelled to Thunder Bay over the weekend and said the province was willing to spend whatever was necessary to fight the fires.
However, First Nations leaders, including from the Anishinabek Nation, accused the premier of being unclear about what support the province was providing and, and of disorganisation in coordinating with First Nations.
The CBC has reported that although Ontario spent $271m on emergency firefighting in 2025-26, it plans to spend only $150m in 2026-27.
The Ontario government did not respond to requests for comment.
First Nations communities are acutely vulnerable to wildfire danger in Canada, with 80% of Indigenous communities located in areas more susceptible to fires, according to a 2019 study from the Journal of Disaster Risk Reduction. The Namaygoosisagagun First Nation faces an additional challenge in that, although it is recognised as a nation by many other First Nations, it is still in the process of being officially recognised by the federal government, making it more difficult to gain emergency funding.
Debassige said Canada’s federal government had agreed to provide the funding for now but that the Anishinabek Nation had had to step in and offer financial support because of delays on the government side.
The Whitewater Lake First Nation, about 250km north of Thunder Bay, was also destroyed by the recent wildfires. Though the community is made up of mostly seasonal residences with no full-time residents, First Nations leaders say the community’s infrastructure is now gone.
Nicole Redvers, an associate professor at Western University in London, Ontario, said there was a disproportionate wildfire impact on Indigenous communities due to proximity to traditional territories that livelihoods are based around, which include forests.
That vulnerability, alongside Canada’s lack of planning around community resilience on climate change, made for scenarios like what the Namaygoosisagagun had to contend with, said Redvers.
“A community had to evacuate themselves without any warning,” she said. “If we don’t have the preparedness capacity within Canada to ensure that all communities have climate adaption plans in place … we’re definitely not well placed to have resilience within our communities going forward.”

full_text:
The likelihood of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike has doubled according to market forecasts, as the escalating Middle East crisis once again drives fuel prices higher amid dwindling global oil reserves.
The total breakdown in the fragile ceasefire between the United States and Iran has sent the international Brent crude benchmark surging by 23% over the past two weeks and back within reach of $US90 a barrel.
As experts warn the global energy market is now at a “critical juncture”, Australian motorists are once again faced with climbing fuel costs, albeit without the panicked buying and accompanying shortages that accompanied the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in early March.
Diesel, which has consistently been most exposed to the global disruptions, has jumped by 40 cents in July to about $2.10 a litre in the major cities on the east coast, according to Motormouth.
The removal of some of the federal government’s fuel excise relief from the start of this month has also contributed to higher costs, with unleaded petrol up by 25 cents to about $1.75.
Amid already depleted global oil stockpiles, analysts warn of a coming tipping point after Iran’s leader declared “full-scale war” with the United States and Houthi rebels threatened to blockade millions of Saudi Arabian oil passing through the Red Sea.
Luke Yeaman, the CBA’s chief economist, said a total lack of trust between the warring parties made it difficult to judge the trajectory of the escalating conflict, which he said would send a fresh stagflationary pulse through the Australian economy.
“In the current dynamic, we believe this will drag on for at least several weeks and possibly longer,” Yeaman said.
With inflation already tracking too high for comfort, traders in financial markets are upping bets that the Reserve Bank could be forced to hike rates for a fourth time.
Markets now place a nearly 30% chance of an interest rate rise on 12 August, up from 16% two weeks ago. The probability of a hike by November has doubled to 80% over the same period, according to ANZ.
Yeaman said he was sticking to his forecast for no more rate rises this year – at least for now.
“If we see a prolonged closure of the strait and a big jump in oil prices, that will feed through to higher inflation, but it will also slow growth. In the short term that could mean the case for one further rate hike is higher.
“But calls for multiple … rate hikes are a little overblown.”
Yeaman warned that global oil prices could push as high as $US150 a barrel if no negotiated solution was reached by late August or early September, conjuring the spectre of worst-case scenarios contemplated during the first phase of the conflict.
“Our expectation is that before some of those extreme points are reached that there is some resolution. I expect that if oil prices really spiked again then the government would step in and shield households by reinstating the full fuel excise discount.”
Regardless, higher energy prices and renewed global conflict is set to further drag on an Australian economy that is already slowing sharply under the additional weight of three interest rate hikes and a falling housing market.
Yeaman said he had forecast economic growth to slow to 1.5% by the end of this year, from 2.5% in 2025.
“Were you to see a serious escalation in the conflict and a prolonged closure of the strait [of Hormuz], then growth could slow much more sharply.”
Daniel Hynes, a senior commodity strategist at ANZ, said the drop in oil prices during the ceasefire into the low 70s had not reflected the structural hit to global supply and the system’s “fragility”, and that $US80 to $90 a barrel was a more realistic level.
“The $US100-a-barrel mark would potentially be within sight if we are here in a few weeks’ time and things have gotten worse.”
Hynes said there were “technical” limits to how low oil inventories could go without triggering a breakdown of infrastructure, and that these limits were already being breached in the United States.
That would push buyers in the US to look further afield for oil, increasing competition for scarce seaborne cargoes and driving up prices.
“At the moment there’s a feeling that if it [renewed conflict] doesn’t persist too much longer, they will be able to suffer through this period without too much damage,” Hynes said.
“Obviously the risks rise day by day; the market is at a critical juncture.”

title: The Queensland government promised to put victims first. Instead it buried a report from domestic violence survivors
summary:
Exclusive: Report from LNP-convened panel heavily criticises police responses to family violence and calls for civilian oversight

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Queensland government has buried the findings of its own working group of domestic violence victim-survivors, after their report was heavily critical of police responses and called for a “civilian review mechanism” to escalate complaints about police.

The Liberal National government has repeatedly said it would “put victims at the heart” of the state’s justice policies.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Queensland government has buried the findings of its own working group of domestic violence victim-survivors, after their report was heavily critical of police responses and called for a “civilian review mechanism” to escalate complaints about police.
The Liberal National government has repeatedly said it would “put victims at the heart” of the state’s justice policies.
In early 2025, the government convened a panel of people with lived experience of domestic, family and sexual violence to identify gaps in the system and guide reforms.
A statement announcing the working group, released by the domestic and family violence prevention minister, Amanda Camm, criticised the former Labor government and said it had “failed to implement recommendations” related to the issue.
The working group concluded its work in December, but a summary report including its recommendations has never been publicly released. Camm’s office refused a Guardian request to release the report this week.
Guardian Australia has seen a copy of the summary report, which noted it was “developed for broader distribution” and to address any concerns related to victim-survivor confidentiality.
Panel members say they cannot speak publicly about the process. One source said on condition of anonymity: “You can say all that you want about being tough on crime and putting victims first, but if it doesn’t come with CCTV footage for the news, then it’s clearly not a government priority.”.
Sources familiar with the process believe the government’s reluctance to release the report and its findings relates to the document’s prominent and strong criticisms of police, including calls for independent oversight.
Since the LNP came to office, the Queensland Police Service has scrapped its specialist domestic and family violence command, and released a reform plan that said domestic and family violence case management was not “core business”. Police have been given additional powers to issue “on the spot” directions that have seriously concerned women’s advocates.
At the same time, the recommendations from several reports that have raised concern about police responses to domestic violence have stalled. These include a long-overdue recommendation to establish a civilian-led police integrity unit to handle complaints.
The leaked report by the victim-survivor working group devotes its first and most detailed section to policing. It said police responses were “inconsistent” and affected by “limited understanding and attitudinal concerns”.
It said policing responses were often dictated by individual officer attitudes rather than “consistent operational approaches”.
“Victim-survivors reported delays in police responses, reporting processes and follow up actions,” it said.
“Some members felt breaches of DVOs were minimised or not treated with the level of seriousness expected.
“An entrenched culture within policing was highlighted as a concern, characterised by inconsistent identification of breaches, and the application of personal judgement, undermining consistent and appropriate responses for victim-survivors.”
The panel made several recommendations in relation to police responses, including calls for the state to adopt nationally standard risk assessment tools and better victim-centred practices.
It also called for “a civilian review mechanism for escalating concerns about inadequate police responses”.
The report also made wide-ranging recommendations about the need for reforms to child protection, mental health, housing, the legal system, and specialist domestic and family violence services. It called for “efforts to address ongoing experiences of systemic racism”.
Guardian Australia approached Camm on Monday asking why no report or recommendations had been made public, and if the minister would release them.
 Her office refused the request and did not provide a written response.
Asked again about the report on Tuesday, Camm did not address questions about why the report had not been released.
She sent a statement that said the government had made a “record high” investment in domestic and family violence prevention and that the government planned to deliver more services, police and affordable housing.
 “It is correct to report, following Labor’s decade of decline, the Crisafulli Government has given a voice to victims of domestic and family violence and has prioritised turning around the deteriorating services we inherited from the former government,” Camm said.
“For example, our government has increased DV Connect’s answer rate from 41.9% under Labor to 84%.”
One source familiar with the report said they believed it was “very clear” that the government’s reluctance to release the summary report was because they were “unwilling to act on many of the recommendations”, especially those related to police.
 “You can’t be for victims, but only when it suits your agenda,” the source said.
Since the 2024 election, the Crisafulli government has taken a hardline and “victim first” approach to youth crime, including several tranches of legal reforms.
At the same time, critics said the government had done comparatively little to address gender-based violence. Funding for domestic and family violence prevention was cut in the recent state budget, and community sector workers said their services were overburdened and under-resourced.

title: ‘Sit down!’: Australian MP yells at dog then snaps at presenter in live interview
summary:
Barnaby Joyce had been defending One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s ‘working holiday’ on ABC current affairs show

The Australian politician Pauline Hanson – a populist, hard-right figure in the Nigel Farage mould – probably expected her European tour to generate headlines.

But the One Nation party leader, who is riding high in the polls, could not have anticipated that coverage would become dominated by one of her MPs yelling at his dog on national television.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Australian politician Pauline Hanson – a populist, hard-right figure in the Nigel Farage mould – probably expected her European tour to generate headlines.
But the One Nation party leader, who is riding high in the polls, could not have anticipated that coverage would become dominated by one of her MPs yelling at his dog on national television.
Hanson’s itinerary in Europe had included holidaying in Italy with the mining billionaire Gina Rinehart, speaking at a conservative conference in London and joining the far-right agitator and convicted criminal Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, who calls himself Tommy Robinson, for a cosy chat on his podcast.
On Monday night, One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce beamed into the ABC’s 7.30 programme from his home in New South Wales to defend Hanson’s European gaffe-filled “working holiday” and her vitriolic comments.
However, the MP’s attempt to mop up some of the mess ended up being overshadowed by an aggressive confrontation with his dog, Stella.
Joyce, a former deputy prime minister and turncoat MP who left the mainstream conservative National party for the more rightwing One Nation in December last year, is no stranger to the limelight. Nor was Monday’s outburst the first time the politician has made the news overseas for a dog-related story, after his run-in with Johnny Depp’s pets in 2015.
About halfway through the tense interview on Monday, the 7.30 host, Sarah Ferguson, put to Joyce that his defection to One Nation was “dragging” him “further into a place of intolerance and racial discrimination”. Ferguson continued: “You’re defending your leader, but are you really comfortable with where she is taking you?”
Joyce’s eyes could be seen darting off-screen during the question. He began answering before suddenly yelling: “Sit down!”
“Sorry. It’s the dog,” he said, before continuing his answer without addressing the substance of Ferguson’s question, instead noting One Nation’s growing polling support.
Joyce later apologised for the dog, which he said was interrupting him. Ferguson said: “Don’t worry about the dog. Just answer the question.” The MP responded: “Don’t be rude. Otherwise, this interview will come to a grinding halt.”
Joyce later told the Guardian that Stella, a “staffy-border collie” cross, had been “barking incessantly” under the deck where he was standing for the interview.
With about 30% of the primary vote according to the latest Newspoll, One Nation is on roughly equal footing with Labor, the centre-left party that holds a majority government in Australia.
Joyce, who has represented the regional NSW electorate of New England as an MP since 2013 and spent nearly a decade as a senator for Queensland before that, is a veteran of both parliament and going viral.
In 2024, while he was still a National party MP, Daily Mail Australia published night-time footage of Joyce in Canberra lying face-up on the pavement with his feet on a planter box, having a phone conversation and uttering profanities.
Joyce also caused a stir in 2019 with a video he posted on X, then Twitter, captioned “Merry Christmas”. Filmed in selfie-mode in a paddock, it involved him declaring he was “sick of the government being in my life” while musing on climate change.
In previous dog-related drama, when Joyce was agriculture minister in 2015, he made the Hollywood actors Depp and Amber Heard film themselves apologising for trying to bring their dogs – Pistol and Boo – into the country against Australia’s strict biosecurity laws.

title: Stand still, make eye contact: Denmark tells tourists how to behave in a wolf encounter
summary:
Government urges visitors not to approach or feed wolves as it manages safety amid growing population

Danish authorities have advised tourists to stand still, make eye contact and put up “maximum resistance” in the event of attack if they encounter a wolf while on holiday.

After a 200-year absence, wolves started returning to Denmark in 2012. There are now estimated to be 49 wolves on the Danish peninsula of Jutland.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Danish authorities have advised tourists to stand still, make eye contact and put up “maximum resistance” in the event of attack if they encounter a wolf while on holiday.
After a 200-year absence, wolves started returning to Denmark in 2012. There are now estimated to be 49 wolves on the Danish peninsula of Jutland.
Generally, it is rare for wolves to even approach humans, but in the area around the popular tourism destination of Oksbøl, young ones were spotted doing so earlier this year.
The municipality of Varde and Visit Vesterhavet have distributed flyers containing the government advice around holiday homes, campsites and tourist offices in Danish, English and German.
Tourists are told to keep calm and still in the presence of a wolf, hold eye contact, take a picture of the animal and, if it will not go away of its own accord, shout, clap hands and wave arms. They are advised not to follow or to turn their backs on an approaching wolf. The tip is to “stare directly at it” to “show dominance”.
While there have been no wolf attacks on humans in Denmark, in the event of it happening, tourists are urged: “You must offer maximum resistance: hit and kick and use any blunt weapon.”
The government advice also states that children under the age of 10 should be accompanied by an adult in the Oksbøl area.
Wolves have long had a presence in Denmark – the oldest wolf bones in the country are 13,000 years old – but after the last wolf was shot in 1813 they only started to make a comeback in the last two decades.
Their presence has received a mixed response, often dividing people along political lines. In April, two ponies were killed by wolves in a fortnight. Soon after, four MPs from the far-right Danish People’s party were reported to police for sharing a Facebook post calling on people to “Shoot the wolf”.
Wolves are protected by EU law.
The wolf expert Peter Sunde, a wildlife ecology professor at Aarhus University, said: “During the winter and spring of 2026, at least two young wolves were observed approaching humans and exhibiting markedly reduced flight distances in the area around Oksbøl that is a tourist hotspot. One of these wolves is still alive.”
This type of behaviour, he said, usually happens when young wolves are repeatedly exposed to humans. “It has been discussed whether tourists, who may be unaware both of the presence of wolves in the area and of the basic recommendations regarding wolf encounters, may have contributed to the development of this behaviour,” he added.
“To prevent similar behaviour from developing in future generations of young wolves, it is important that people who live in or visit wolf habitats – including tourists – understand that they should neither approach wolves nor leave food that may attract them.”
Varde’s second deputy mayor, Sandie Eis Ravn, said the campaign was aimed at informing tourists at the request of local businesses. “If you are visiting somewhere and you know there is a wolf in the nearby forest, to make sure you have the right code of conduct when you meet this creature,” she said.

title: What the EU wants from Andy Burnham
summary:
European leaders have made positive noises about the new UK PM, but he is likely to face the same restrictions as Starmer

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Andy Burnham is unknown in Brussels, but that will soon change. In his schedule for the autumn is an EU-UK summit that may underscore the same dilemmas that have confronted previous British prime ministers in the relationship with Europe.

EU leaders were quick to offer congratulations to Britain’s prime minister, the seventh since the 2016 Brexit referendum. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to strengthening the EU-UK partnership “for the security of our shared continent” and “the prosperity of people on both sides of the Channel”. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, invited Burnham to visit Berlin “very soon”, noting that the UK and Germany’s “deep connection is particularly evident in these times”.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Andy Burnham is unknown in Brussels, but that will soon change. In his schedule for the autumn is an EU-UK summit that may underscore the same dilemmas that have confronted previous British prime ministers in the relationship with Europe.
EU leaders were quick to offer congratulations to Britain’s prime minister, the seventh since the 2016 Brexit referendum. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she looked forward to strengthening the EU-UK partnership “for the security of our shared continent” and “the prosperity of people on both sides of the Channel”. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, invited Burnham to visit Berlin “very soon”, noting that the UK and Germany’s “deep connection is particularly evident in these times”.
Georg Riekeles, a former adviser on the commission’s Brexit taskforce, told the Guardian: “People don’t know what to expect. But he also starts with a blank sheet of paper … and that can be an advantage.”
The main concern, said Riekeles, who is now an associate director at the European Policy Centre, was whether Burnham would be “on the same trajectory” in terms of defence and security cooperation, energy and the “very positive agenda” on economic issues.
One EU diplomat observed: “For a British prime minister it is not necessarily a bad thing to be little known. If you are well known it is probably because you were prominent on one side or the other of the Brexit debate.”
Burnham’s most notable statement on the EU was his wish to see Britain rejoin in his lifetime, while speaking to the Guardian at the Labour party conference in September 2025. But during campaigning in the leave-voting constituency of Makerfield, he made it clear reversing Brexit was not a priority, because “Britain would be stuck in a permanent rut if we are just constantly arguing”.
Michael Jacobs, who advised the former prime minister Gordon Brown, said Burnham’s statement on rejoining “felt like it was from the heart” but was also politically astute. “It tells pro-Europeans that he is one of them. But it tells leave voters that it’s not his political priority for now, and he is not going to relitigate the Brexit arguments.”
Among the first calls Burnham had after entering No 10 were with von der Leyen, Merz and the French leader, Emmanuel Macron.
He has appointed Hamish Falconer as the Europe minister, replacing Nick Thomas-Symonds. The latter’s departure is a blow to the UK-EU reset talks started by Starmer, but some claimed they had lost momentum and Falconer would bring fresh energy. One of his first calls after being appointed was to the European trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič.
Elected as an MP in 2024, Falconer brings a wealth of international experience, with a decade spent in the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a stint in the National Crime Agency, and a career dealing with international terrorism, hostage recovery and countering human trafficking.
He served as Middle East minister under Starmer.
The return of Johnny Reynolds, as business secretary, will help in talks aimed at protecting European trade from China, and tricky negotiations to scrap an upcoming 10% tariff on exports of British cars to the EU and vice versa.
Under Starmer, the UK and EU signed a security and defence pact and cooperated closely on Ukraine. Despite failing to agree British participation in a €150bn EU defence loans scheme, the two sides moved on. In Starmer’s final week in office the UK signed an agreement to participate in the EU’s €90bn (£77bn) loan for Ukraine, meaning British companies can provide more weapons funded through the scheme.
Now Burnham inherits the reset agenda launched by Starmer. The two sides are due to sign a trio of agreements at the summit: a deal to reduce paperwork and certification for fresh food in an effort to ease trade barriers for British exporters; linking emissions trading systems; and a youth exchange scheme enabling 18- to 30-year-olds to work, study, travel and volunteer in the EU and UK.
Ireland’s Europe minister, Thomas Byrne, told reporters this month that he expected “positive continuity, at the very least”.
Ireland, which holds the EU Council’s rotating presidency until the end of the year, will be involved in the diplomatic preparations for the summit, the date of which is yet to be decided. “There are tricky issues there, and I think we can get them over the line,” Byrne said.
Talks have been deadlocked over the youth mobility agreement. EU member states think the UK’s proposed cap of 50,000 youth visas is too low and they oppose their nationals paying the NHS surcharge and higher rate of tuition fees for foreign students. But Some diplomats see a middle ground whereby EU students get a discount on foreign fees but pay above the domestic rate.
Jacobs suggested Burnham may raise the cap on numbers. “The idea that leave voters regard such a scheme as a form of immigration was always slightly absurd, and I think Burnham will see that as a relatively easy win to offer pro-Europeans.”
But when it comes to the UK-EU economic relationship, Burnham will face the same constraints as Starmer.
Earlier this year the EU rejected an attempt by Starmer to negotiate a single market for goods, minus the free movement of people. EU member states suggested the UK could join the European Economic Area, but that would require accepting the free movement of people and making payments to the EU budget with no voting rights in shaping new EU rules.
Jacobs said: “Given Burnham’s sensitivity to the immigration concerns of his own Makerfield voters, and of many others, the idea that he would seek to re-enter the single market by allowing free movement and making a massive financial payment to the EU budget (which is what the EU would demand) seems implausible.
“On the substantive issues, I think he will do pretty much what Starmer has been trying to do with the so-called ‘reset’, and he will come up against the same barriers in Brussels.”

title: ‘No electricity, no water, no fuel’: Ukrainian drone strikes bring darkness to Crimea’s summer
summary:
Interviews with residents of Russian-held region point to frustration with Moscow as Ukrainian campaign to isolate it takes toll on daily life

First, the guests stopped coming. As Ukrainian drones and missiles pounded Crimea throughout the spring and into the summer, Russian tourists began cancelling their bookings at the small guesthouse Marina runs in Yevpatoria, a resort town on the peninsula’s Black Sea coast.

Then petrol became scarce, making it harder to stock the business with food and other essentials. Now, electricity and running water are cut off for much of the day, just as the summer heat sets in.

Continue reading...
full_text:
First, the guests stopped coming. As Ukrainian drones and missiles pounded Crimea throughout the spring and into the summer, Russian tourists began cancelling their bookings at the small guesthouse Marina runs in Yevpatoria, a resort town on the peninsula’s Black Sea coast.
Then petrol became scarce, making it harder to stock the business with food and other essentials. Now, electricity and running water are cut off for much of the day, just as the summer heat sets in.
“For 12 years they told us Crimea was 100% protected,” Marina said, referring to the promises Russian officials have made since seizing it from Ukraine in 2014. “And then, within a month, we’ve been thrown back into the Stone Age – no electricity, no water, no fuel.”
Since the start of this year, Kyiv has launched its largest sustained air campaign against Crimea, targeting both the peninsula and the land and sea transport links connecting it to Russia. Residents are facing the most severe disruption to daily life since its annexation in 2014.
It was the first Russian-controlled region to experience the acute motor fuel shortages that have since spread to Russia. The Kremlin-installed authorities last month declared a state of emergency and temporarily banned sales to private motorists in an effort to preserve supplies for the military and emergency services.
But as Ukrainian drones increasingly targeted the peninsula’s energy infrastructure, the crisis has quickly moved beyond petrol. More than 70% of Crimea’s roughly 2.5 million residents have experienced some form of power outage, according to a Guardian analysis, while many have now gone several consecutive days without electricity or running water.
Interviews with more than a dozen residents across Crimea pointed to a growing sense of abandonment and frustration with both the Russian-installed authorities and Moscow, as Kyiv seeks to turn the peninsula “into an island”.
The festivals, summer camps and beach events that once filled Crimea’s season have been cancelled. In their place, long queues for petrol and a daily search for somewhere to shower and charge a phone. “We’re surviving, not living,” one resident said.
Aleksei, a Crimean native who supported Russia’s annexation of the peninsula in 2014, says his restaurant has been largely empty this summer as tourists stayed away, while shortages and disrupted supply routes have made it increasingly difficult to source fresh produce from outside the peninsula.
“The authorities kept insisting Crimea was ready for anything. Literally anything. It turns out the authorities failed to prepare for the worst,” he says. “People are hunting for fuel like it’s The Hunger Games.”
Like others interviewed by the Guardian, Aleksei asked for his surname to be withheld for security reasons. Crimea is home to one of Russia’s most pervasive and repressive security apparatuses that has left many people fearful of speaking openly. Public expressions of dissent are rare.
Comments beneath officials’ social media posts have, however, become flooded with pleas for help from people who say they cannot contact relatives, buy food or cope with the prolonged outages.
“Belogorsk has been without electricity for more than 70 hours, and all we keep getting are promises,” read one of dozens of comments addressed to Crimea’s Russian-installed head, Sergei Aksyonov.
Local Telegram chats have turned into improvised survival guides, with residents swapping tips on where fuel has just arrived, setting alarms for late-night voucher releases, sharing maps of the shortest queues and informing each other which neighbourhoods still have electricity or running water.
Since it was seized by Russia in 2014 amid the turmoil of Ukraine’s Maidan revolution, which ousted the country’s pro-Russian president, Crimea has been transformed into one of the Kremlin’s most strategically important territories.
In 2022, it became the main staging ground for the invasion of southern Ukraine, where Russian forces advanced far more rapidly than in their failed assault on Kyiv. Since the full-scale invasion, its military infrastructure has been used for air attacks and battlefield support. Moscow has also encouraged hundreds of thousands of Russians to settle on the peninsula.
The 2014 annexation – of what for many Russians is seen as a desirable region of warm weather and beaches – sent Vladimir Putin’s approval ratings soaring and, for years, annual celebrations marking Crimea’s “return” served as choreographed displays of Russian military power and national resurgence.
By targeting Crimea – long held up by the Kremlin as the crown jewel of Putin’s rule – Ukraine hopes to strengthen its hand in any future peace negotiations, says Rob Lee, a military analyst and senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute.
“Ukraine has more leverage in future negotiations than it did before because it can now reliably strike almost any target in Crimea.”
Ukraine has focused its strikes on the main transport routes supplying Crimea, particularly the Novorossiya highway, a key logistics corridor linking the peninsula to Russia’s Rostov region through the occupied cities of Melitopol and Mariupol.
Ukrainian forces struck more than 240 Russian military trucks during the first week of July alone, according to an analysis of verified strike footage by the French open-source intelligence analyst Clément Molin.
More recently, Ukraine has escalated its campaign against Russian shipping in the Sea of Azov. Over the last week, Kyiv’s military said it had struck 90 vessels used by Russia to supply the occupied peninsula.
In a recent interview with the independent Russian journalist Dmitry Kolezev, an unnamed Russian general said Ukraine’s recent successes were partly the result of Moscow diverting resources away from defending Crimea and towards its offensive in the Donbas.
With the military leadership fixated on capturing the remaining parts of the Donbas, the general said, Crimea had slipped to “third or fourth” on Russia’s list of priorities.
Lee says Ukraine has succeeded in producing large numbers of medium- and long-range drones, making it increasingly difficult for Russia to defend against them all. “The cost of these drones is low enough that it’s not prohibitively expensive for Ukraine to keep launching these attacks,” he said.
Military analysts on both sides believe Ukraine is likely to intensify its campaign in the coming weeks against the Kerch Bridge, which opened in 2018 to link Crimea to Russia, in an effort to deepen the peninsula’s mounting shortages.
Successes in isolating Crimea have provided Ukraine with a much-needed morale boost at a time when Russian forces continue to make slow but steady gains on the battlefield, most recently advancing to the brink of capturing the strategically important city of Kostiantynivka in eastern Ukraine.
For Moscow, the crisis on the peninsula is an embarrassment it can neither hide nor easily fix. The Kremlin instead has sought to play down the crisis.
During a meeting with senior officials last week, Putin instructed the government to urgently provide subsidies to Crimea and Sevastopol to finance fuel purchases and lower petrol prices on the peninsula. “These are temporary problems,” he said.
But in Crimea, many residents said the Kremlin’s reassurances only deepened their frustration. “They keep telling us these are only temporary problems,” said Dmitry, a university student. “We’ve been living like this for weeks. This isn’t normal life, and it can’t go on much longer.”

title: Zendaya faces backlash for wearing ancient Iranian jewellery at Odyssey event
summary:
Film star promotes Christopher Nolan film epic wearing gold artefacts dating back almost 3,000 years

The Odyssey is a story about a Greek king’s long journey home. But a pair of earrings worn on the new film adaptation’s press tour – and their long separation from their homeland – is sparking controversy.

At a photocall in London, Zendaya, who plays the goddess Athena in the Christopher Nolan film, wore a pair of earrings fashioned from Iranian artefacts dating back to 700BC.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The Odyssey is a story about a Greek king’s long journey home. But a pair of earrings worn on the new film adaptation’s press tour – and their long separation from their homeland – is sparking controversy.
At a photocall in London, Zendaya, who plays the goddess Athena in the Christopher Nolan film, wore a pair of earrings fashioned from Iranian artefacts dating back to 700BC.
The backlash was swift, with archaeologists criticising the use of precious and culturally significant artefacts as accessories in the promotion of a Hollywood film, claiming it was a “hijacking” of Iran’s contributions to humanity.
The earrings belong to Barron London, a Mayfair-based gallery and dealer whose website states: “With a reputation for discretion, the gallery works privately with collectors, estates and institutions to uncover and place pieces of significance.”
According to a formal statement from Barron the artefacts, which were bought from another London jeweller, Glenn Spiro, in 2025, “are attributed to the Ziwiye hoard, discovered in north-western Iran in the late 1940s”.
The hoard was a trove of gold, silver, bronze and terracotta found in 1947 and looted by shepherds. According to a 2015 research paper, the surviving pieces were “sold in antique markets out of Iran in the 1960s” and “are now scattered in different museums and private collections”.
Prof Sussan Babaie, an Iranian-born art historian and Courtauld Institute professor, said it was “shocking to see that no one thought maybe this is not a good idea”.
Expressing “outrage” that Zendaya was wearing the ancient objects, she said: “There is not enough cultural knowledge and cultural sensibility among those who dress [celebrities], those who accessorise them, those who put them up as the symbols of beauty and power and an expression of the movie’s high-mindedness.” Representatives for Zendaya and her stylist have been contacted for comment.
The row comes amid scrutiny of western institutions that hold ancient artefacts. The British Museum has faced criticism over its looted Benin bronzes, sacred Ethiopian altar tablets and the Parthenon marbles.
Kim Kardashian wore a dress that belonged to Marilyn Monroe at the Met Gala in 2022. As Scott Fortner, who has a collection of Monroe artefacts, told the BBC at the time: “When you buy something of such significance, you really need to stick to your word to protect and preserve it … and clearly that didn’t happen.” The gown’s owners denied that any damage had been done to the dress.
Dr Annelise Baer, an archaeologist and producer whose video about Zendaya’s earrings garnered criticism for what some perceived as condoning the use of the artefacts, said the main ethical issue was “that the earrings themselves are made out of looted antiquities”.
She added: “Zendaya wearing them is kind of a secondary fact … but because she has worn them on a red carpet for a major international movie premiere, this has suddenly put all of that into the public eye in a way that we haven’t really seen before.”
According to Barron’s statement, the earrings “are responsibly stewarded in accordance with their documented provenance and all applicable legal requirements”.
Babaie said the jewellery probably had “extremely important spiritual connotations”, adding: “These are objects that are not meant to be displayed as accessories… It’s human heritage. It’s world heritage, not just accessories.”
The effect, she said, was to strip the earrings “of all meaning”. It is, she claims, “hijacking, flattening and transforming [ancient Iran’s] cultural contributions to humanity”.
The timing is also causing further anger. Babaie highlighted a “maddening” situation in which the press tour for The Odyssey is “glamourising the antiquities of Iran … just as billions of American dollars are being used to bomb Iran”, destroying sites of cultural and historical interest.
In its statement, Barron added: “The intention behind the loan was never commercial. It was to celebrate the remarkable artistry of ancient Persian goldsmiths and to encourage wider appreciation of one of the world’s great artistic traditions. At a time when Iran is so often represented through the lens of contemporary politics, we hope these earrings can also remind audiences of the country’s profound cultural, artistic and historical legacy.”
The Odyssey has also been criticised over one of its filming locations. Sahrawi film-makers are calling for a boycott of the movie over the use of the city of Dakhla in occupied Western Sahara – a stretch of land under Moroccan control sometimes referred to as “Africa’s last colony”.

title: America's Summer Camps Are Facing a New Climate Reality. Here's How They're Adapting
summary: From extreme heat and wildfires to intense flooding, America's summer camps are facing a new reality.
full_text:
Anna Ellena-Rosenau remembers summers at Mountain Meadow Ranch Summer Camp, founded by her grandfather 70 years ago. Nestled in the Sierra Nevada Mountains of California, the weather was always mild—with high temperatures usually contained to one or two
“When I was a camper, we would come to our campfire with jeans and sweatshirts and beanies because it would get so cool,” says Ellena-Rosenau, now the camp’s director. “Now, you could do the whole campfire in your shorts and a tank top.”
In a warming world, summer camp is not what it used to be. The last 11 years have all been among the
observed in instrumental record and perhaps at no time is that more apparent than in the summer. Summer camps around the U.S. are reckoning with how to safely prioritize outdoor play amid
—from wildfires, to record breaking temperatures, to stronger summer storms.
Most camps have always had plans in place for extreme weather. “This is not new for camps that are typically outdoors, in the summer, and in warmer climates,” says Henry DeHart, CEO of the American Camp Association (ACA). “There have always been days where the heat index has gotten high. Now, what’s happening is that the instances of this are increasing. From a camp planning perspective, whether you're dealing with five days of extreme heat in the summer or 8 or 10 days, you still have a plan to deal with it.”
But after flooding killed 28 people, including 25 campers, last summer at Camp Mystic in Texas, more and more parents are concerned about camp safety plans and security. “Every family I talked to during the off season, that was the number one question,” says Brooks Johnson, director of Brown Ledge Camp in Colchester, Vt.; over the past few years the Green Mountain State has also seen its share of flooding.
ACA-accredited camps like Mountain Meadow and Brown Ledge are required to have plans in place for extreme weather events like wildfires and floods, says DeHart. “Our goal at ACA is to make sure camps have good plans in place so that their campers and staff can be safe, because kids need these experiences more than ever,” he says. “In the age of the internet and phones and social media, kids are outside less, they’re active less, and they're building face-to-face relationships less. Camp is more important now than ever, and climate impacts are increasing, and so [they] have to be really vigilant about having good plans related to that.”
For Johnson, part of that has involved coordinating with local officials on evacuation areas, and having a structural engineer ensure that buildings are storm ready. “It's a lot of planning to prepare for the worst and hoping that you never have to use it,” he says.
But on the day-to-day, activity periods are now shorter, and campers spend more time in the pool or doing other aquatic activities. “There was one day where it was too hot to ride [horses], so they put their boots and bathing suits on and bathed the horses,” says Johnson.
At Mountain Meadow, water bottles are now used as passes to activities to ensure kids always have their water bottles on them and are staying hydrated. The camp no longer offers a session in August—when temperatures are highest and the wildfire risk is greatest. In 2021 and 2024, they were forced to cancel sessions due to wildfire smoke.
Things might look a little different from when she was a kid, but Ellena-Rosenau notes that that's just how it goes at camp. “Camp is about adapting and being flexible,” she says. “It's been 70 years of this camp, and every summer we're tweaking and evaluating and finding new ways to beat the heat.”

title: Is Lettuce Safe to Eat? The Latest on the Cyclosporiasis Outbreak
summary: The FDA backpedaled on a positive Cyclospora test result, but the agency says iceberg lettuce remains a suspect.
full_text:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said on Sunday, July 19, that a test that appeared to find
in shredded iceberg lettuce was actually a “
The FDA previously said that laboratory testing had identified
, the parasite responsible for a
multistate diarrhea outbreak
that has sickened thousands, in a sample of shredded iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico. But after reviewing the sample results again, the agency said it was revising its announcement.
“Due to the complexity in detection of
, FDA laboratory experts…have concluded that the finding does not represent true amplification and should be considered a false positive,” the agency
wrote in a July 20 post on X
. FDA officials stressed, however, that Taylor Farms locations in Mexico and iceberg lettuce remain linked to the outbreak despite the false positive result.
Here’s what else you should know about the cyclosporiasis outbreak and what you can do to protect yourself.
Federal health officials previously linked shredded iceberg lettuce
supplied by Taylor Farms to Taco Bell restaurants
in five states to at least 1,600 cyclosporiasis
On Saturday, July 18, the FDA
(in a page that has since been deleted) that a sample of Taylor Farms shredded iceberg lettuce had tested positive for
. The sample was collected as part of the agency’s outbreak investigation from a batch of imported products at the southern border, the FDA said. The following day, the agency said the test had been a false positive. It later stressed that Taylor Farms lettuce remained implicated as a potential source of the outbreak despite the testing error.
The FDA said in the post on X that its “traceback investigation and outbreak data,” including interviews with people sickened by
, “continue to converge on shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms locations in central Mexico.”
“To clarify, this false-positive lab sample DOES NOT change the basis for FDA’s ongoing outbreak investigation or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the current voluntary recall by Taylor Farms,” the FDA post said.
Taylor Farms, a major lettuce supplier to U.S. supermarkets and fast-food chains,
Sunday that it had voluntarily recalled its iceberg lettuce grown and processed in central Mexico “in an abundance of caution.”
The company added that the FDA had “apologized” for its testing mistake. An FDA official said at a press conference Monday that the agency had not apologized to Taylor Farms, but had notified the company of the results of its testing process.
Even if iceberg lettuce is confirmed as a source of some cyclosporiasis cases, it might not be the only culprit of infections across the country, says Don Schaffner, a food-science expert at Rutgers University.
The FDA said at a press conference on Monday that it has investigated multiple clusters of cyclosporiasis cases since May, though the outbreak linked to Taco Bell and Taylor Farms is the largest.
Past cyclosporiasis outbreaks in the U.S. have been linked to fresh produce such as raspberries, cilantro, snow peas, and leafy greens. Cyclosporiasis can also be acquired via contaminated water. “You can get it from a variety of different sources,” Schaffner says. “There’s this correlation with Taco Bell lettuce, but there are probably other outbreaks going on, making it hard to find just one cause.”
What is a “false positive” result?
A false positive happens when a test says something is present, but it actually isn’t. Food-safety experts say a false positive result for
in a food sample is to do a polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, test, Schaffner says. The test works by attempting to find the parasite’s DNA and then amplifying what it finds. “It will keep doubling the DNA until it reaches a detectable signal,” Schaffner says.
But if the sample is compromised or too many cycles of the test are run, “you can also amplify garbage DNA in the sample” that is not from the parasite but is similar enough to fool the test, which could result in a false positive, Schaffner says.
The FDA hasn’t explained how the false positive result came about or why it was reported publicly. The agency has
only that its laboratory experts “re-reviewed” the positive lettuce sample and concluded that the initial finding was incorrect.
is difficult to detect in food, FDA officials have said, and detecting the parasite in iceberg lettuce is particularly tricky as the vegetable’s short shelf-life and the parasite’s long incubation period mean that by the time people are sickened, the contaminated lettuce is usually gone from store shelves and restaurant tables.
So, is it safe to eat lettuce?
The FDA has urged consumers, restaurants, and retailers to discard and not consume all
recalled iceberg lettuce
distributed by Taylor Fresh Foods. The recalled lettuce was distributed from June 29 to July 16 in 27 states.
The FDA also says to avoid eating “recalled lettuce at any Taco Bell location” or other restaurants. “If you don’t know the source of the iceberg lettuce, ask the restaurant,” the agency advises.
To help reduce the risk of cyclosporiasis, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends that people wash all fruits and vegetables under running water, including produce labeled as pre-washed. Firm fruits and vegetables, such as cucumbers and melons, should be scrubbed with a produce brush, the agency says.
Cooking vegetables and fruits to an internal temperature of at least 158°F can
But some food-safety experts say it is probably OK to eat that Caesar salad or burger with shredded greens. Schaffner, the Rutgers expert, says he hasn’t changed his own eating habits and continues to eat salads daily.
“Maybe don’t eat lettuce at Taco Bell in Michigan four weeks ago,” he jokes, referring to the state hard-hit by the
outbreak. Michigan state health officials said on July 21 that
more than 6,500 cases
of cyclosporiasis have been reported in the state since June 22.
“I know people are worried, but I don’t think you need to stop eating fresh produce,” Schaffner says.
Wade Syers, who lives in Michigan and is Michigan State University Extension’s food-safety specialist, says he too is eating lettuce and doesn’t think people need to shy away from fresh fruits and vegetables.
“What I’ve been advising everyone to do is to follow food-safety guidelines, which is what we should be doing anyway: wash your hands before, during and after food prep, for example, and rinse all produce under running water,” he says.
With lettuce, he advises buying a whole head of it and removing the outer leaves before washing the rest thoroughly. Also keep an eye out for recall notices and outbreak updates, he says.
If you do develop symptoms of cyclosporiasis, which include watery and sometimes explosive
, the CDC recommends contacting your doctor, getting tested, and staying hydrated.

title: The CEO Moment: Qualcomm’s Cristiano Amon
summary: Amon talks to TIME editor-in-chief Sam Jacobs about how Qualcomm became a leader in semiconductors, his trip to China with President Trump, and why he thinks doing business is like fighting in the Colosseum.
full_text:
Those who are bullish about the future of artificial intelligence imagine a day soon when consumer products are finally able to match the potential capabilities of the technology. Among the companies determining that future is
, the semiconductor leader whose chips power many of the devices in our lives—from smartphones to automobiles. Cristiano Amon, who marks his fifth anniversary as CEO this summer, is responsible for steering the 41-year-old communications company through a pivotal moment. He recently joined
, our new interview series featuring some of the world’s most influential business leaders, to talk about his trip to China with President Trump, where AI is heading next, and how he plans to keep his company competitive.
You've said, I tell my team, we are in the gladiator business. Do you honestly say that?
The reason I use this analogy is because if you’re a gladiator, you go to the Colosseum, There's going to be three outcomes: You're going to win, you're going to lose, or you're both going to lose. So you go in, you have a 33% chance of success. If you win, the only thing you accomplished, you can go to the Colosseum one more time.
You've also said that whatever people believe
, it's probably going to be bigger. What makes you so sure?
Back in the 2000, people said the internet's going to be big…If you look now, 26 years later, the internet is way bigger than people thought—by an order of magnitude. It's probably been underhyped in the long run.
You envision a world where humans interact with information that moves beyond smartphones. History makes me question this. So far these devices have failed to take off. Can you convince me now that that future that we've been waiting for is finally here?
I have 40 different designs today of people doing personal AI devices. There are companies doing glasses, which is obvious. There’s jewelry, pendants, pens, bracelets, watches…Will all those things pan out? I don't know. I tell you what, right now I'm very comfortable making one bet. Glasses will because this is prime real estate. It's close to my eyes, to my ears, to my mouth.
Is it important for you for Qualcomm to be seen as an AI company?
The future of computing is AI. So by definition, if we're a computing company, we're going to be an AI company. Those things are no longer separable.
You recently accompanied President Trump to
with Chinese President Xi Jinping. What did the trip tell you about the future of the semiconductor supply chain?
I came out of the trip optimistic. There's value in providing semiconductors in American technology stacks to companies in China.
Should Americans be concerned if you sell advanced chips to Chinese companies?
Chips are in everything right now. Chips are in every consumer electronic device and in cars and appliances and everything…It's pretty easy to understand: Do you like American technology for America? Or do you like American technology for the world?
You present it as if there's one obvious choice, but there are lots of people who would disagree with you.
At the end of the day, it's just math…every leading semiconductor company right now has exposure in business in China. That's a good thing.

title: Your Brain Forgets Your Wins. A Brag Folder Can Help
summary: Save your compliments. Future you will need them.
full_text:
saved plenty of things you'll never need again
: old tax returns, the assembly instructions for a bookshelf you built a decade ago, screenshots of recipes you'll never cook.
But when it comes to evidence of what you've done well—whether that's accomplishing something meaningful, helping someone, or growing in ways that matter—most of us keep surprisingly little. Psychologists say that's a missed opportunity. And it’s why many recommend keeping what's known as a brag folder: a
running record of wins
, milestones, and moments of growth that you can revisit when your
gets louder than your memory.
If the idea sounds self-indulgent, experts say it's actually the opposite. A brag folder isn't about inflating your ego so much as giving your brain a more accurate record of your life than it's likely to keep on its own. Here's how to build one you'll actually use—and when you should revisit it.
Why a brag folder works
Cindra Kamphoff, a performance psychologist in Minneapolis, discovered the value of focusing on small wins when her father spent weeks in intensive care after heart surgery. Her family began writing down one "win" each day—sometimes as small as getting a pillow, other days celebrating a medical milestone—and posting the notes on a board in his hospital room. "I have to see something different," she remembers thinking. The "win wall," as she called it, helped her family focus on progress instead of just setbacks and “have more energy to tackle the hard things.” Nurses told them their room felt different from the others on the unit.
The same thing happens in everyday life, just with lower stakes. Most of us spend far more time thinking about what's left to do than taking stock of what we've already done. "It's easy to see how far you have to go instead of celebrating how far you've come," Kamphoff says. A brag folder gives you somewhere to look when your brain insists you've never done anything worth remembering. She thinks of it as a bank account for your self-esteem: Every win you log, however small, is a deposit to draw on the next time self-doubt creeps in. "We think confidence is built by chasing perfection," she says, "but it's really built by recognizing progress."
There's a reason to log a physical or digital record of these things. Atalie Abramovici, a therapist in Los Angeles, points out that our brains naturally scan for threats—a tendency psychologists call the negativity bias. When we're upset, the part of the brain that helps us retrieve evidence to the contrary is harder to access. A brag folder intentionally redirects your attention toward evidence your brain would otherwise overlook. Instead of trying to remember what you're capable of, you can simply look at it.
In a form of counseling called narrative therapy, Abramovici says, this is an established technique known as "unique outcomes." It involves deliberately taking stock of experiences that contradict the negative story you're currently telling yourself. "It's not to feed your ego," she says. "It's just to balance out your appraisal of yourself."
What actually goes in a brag folder
For many people, getting started is the hardest part. It's surprisingly difficult to decide what belongs in a brag folder without feeling like you're...well,
. Adebisi Gbadamosi, a therapist in Deltona, Fla., who works a lot with high-achieving adults, prefers a different approach. When looking back at accomplishments, rather than focusing on what you're proud of now, she suggests asking yourself what excited you them. Which project did you look forward to working on? What challenge did you genuinely enjoy? What kind of work would you jump at the chance to do again? "When you walk through it like that, you’re able to come up with way more accomplishments that you may not have seen as an accomplishment at first," she says.
Once you've identified one, write down four things: the accomplishment itself, why you're proud of it, the value it brought to someone else, and something you learned along the way. The structure does double duty—it gives you language when modesty might otherwise leave you speechless, and it transforms a simple list into a richer reminder of why the experience mattered.
Then collect the receipts, whether they're from your personal or professional life: the email that made your day, the photo from a milestone you worked hard to reach, the handwritten note you couldn't bring yourself to throw away, the text from a friend thanking you for showing up, the review that reminded you your work mattered. If it makes you pause, smile, and think, “I'd forgotten about that,” it probably belongs in your brag folder.
You’re not just creating a more visual resume. Harvind Singh, the CEO of a consulting engineering firm in Chicago, didn't start keeping a brag log until mid-career. When colleagues asked her to pull together a list of accomplishments for an award submission, she realized how much she'd overlooked. Years of committee work, board service, and industry leadership barely registered because they'd simply become part of her job. "Being humble doesn't mean you don't acknowledge what you've done," she says.
She now logs awards and client kudos, but her list also holds the things that come with no certificate at all—like being asked to join a board (even if she had to decline the invitation). Achievements outside of work belong there, too: training for a marathon, signing up for a solo trip, finishing a knitting project, writing a book that nobody published. "You still wrote it,” Singh says.
How to build one you'll keep
Don't overthink the format. Singh keeps an Excel file she calls her brag log, with tabs for career highlights, awards, client testimonials, speaking engagements, publications, and certifications. She's also a fountain pen person who writes anniversary notes to her employees in purple ink, and she'd tell you that a legal pad works fine. If you're more visual, you might prefer a bulletin board or vision board; others like a Google doc or use their iPhone Notes app. "Whether you write it in a book or you use an Excel file, it doesn't really make a difference," she says. Pick whatever you’re most comfortable with.
The bigger challenge is remembering to keep it updated. It's easy to feel motivated the day you create a brag folder, then forget it exists for the next six months. Singh recommends setting a recurring monthly reminder and asking yourself one simple question: “Is there anything I did this month that I want to add?” Without that prompt, "If you don't write it down, you're gonna forget," she says.
And if you're thinking you're years—or even decades—too late to start, you're not. The list fills faster than you'd think, and remembering older entries gets easier once there's somewhere to put them. Plus, it doesn't have to be perfect. "No one's going to grade this," Gbadamosi says. "No one has to see it.”
When to open your brag folder
A brag folder only works if you actually open it. Experts say there are a handful of moments when it can be especially powerful.
The first is when self-doubt starts getting the upper hand. Dr. Linda Dolin, chief medical officer at the Sylvia Brafman Mental Health Center in Fort Lauderdale, recommends revisiting your brag folder during a job loss, a breakup, a rough stretch at work, or any week when your confidence has taken a hit.
thrives on vague feelings—
"I'm not good enough," "I don't belong here."
A brag folder gives you something concrete to push back with. Reading those reminders "anchors your self-worth," Dolin says, helping stop that spiral before it picks up speed.
It's also worth opening before moments that feel intimidating. Abramovici recommends reviewing it ahead of a job interview, a first date, or a conversation in which you'll need to advocate for yourself. The point isn't to psych yourself up with empty affirmations, she says. It's simply to remind yourself of what you already know. Over time, Abramovici says, "it's really b
